Creating Standardized Audit Observation Prompts for Local Fund Audit Reports Introduction Local Fund Audit involves examination of accounts, records, transactions, projects, schemes, and administrative activities of local bodies such as Gram Panchayats (GP), Zilla Parishads (ZP), Nagar Panchayats (NP), and Municipalities.
Audit observations prepared by Local Fund Auditors should be:
Clear and objective. Based on documentary evidence. Focused on control weaknesses. Written in formal audit language. Followed by practical recommendations. A consistent format helps auditors prepare uniform audit reports and ensures that important findings, financial implications, and corrective measures are properly communicated.
This article explains a reusable prompt structure for generating concise and professional audit observations.
Purpose of the Audit Observation Prompt The objective of the prompt is to generate audit paragraphs similar to those prepared by a Local Fund Audit authority while examining:
Public works. Procurement activities. Financial transactions. Grants utilization. Scheme implementation. Asset management. Revenue collection. Establishment matters. Stores and inventory. Records maintenance. The generated observation should identify:
What was noticed during audit. Why the issue occurred. What impact it created. What corrective action should be taken. Standard Audit Observation Structure Each audit observation should contain two parts:
1. Title The title should briefly indicate the nature of the irregularity.
Examples:
Delay in Completion of Road Construction Work. Non-Maintenance of Stock Register. Irregular Procurement of Materials. Unutilized Assets Purchased from Public Funds. Short Recovery of Municipal Revenue. Excess Payment to Contractor. Non-Submission of Utilization Certificates. The title should be short and specific.
2. Body of Observation The observation should be written as a single paragraph.
The paragraph should follow this sequence:
Audit Finding The first part should mention:
Entity audited. Activity examined. Specific irregularity noticed. Relevant amount, quantity, period, or records wherever available. Example:
During the audit of procurement activities of the Nagar Panchayat, it was observed that 150 streetlights amounting to ₹7.50 lakh were procured during FY 2022-23 without proper assessment of actual requirement and without maintaining adequate installation records.
Impact of Finding The second part should explain the consequence of the weakness.
Possible impacts:
Risk of financial loss. Inefficient utilization of public funds. Lack of transparency. Weak internal control. Possibility of misuse of assets. Difficulty in verification. Non-achievement of intended objectives. Example:
The absence of proper planning and monitoring resulted in idle investment of public funds and increased risk of deterioration of unused materials.
Recommendation The last part should suggest corrective action.
The recommendation should be written in passive voice.
Examples:
Proper procurement planning should be ensured. Periodic verification of assets should be carried out. Registers should be maintained regularly. Necessary recovery should be made from responsible persons. Compliance with prescribed rules should be ensured. Example:
It was recommended that future procurements be undertaken only after proper assessment of requirement and that stock verification and utilization monitoring mechanisms be strengthened.
Master Prompt for Generating Audit Observations The following prompt can be used for preparing audit observations for Local Fund Audit reports.
Write a series of concise audit observations in the style of a Local Fund Auditor reviewing local bodies such as:* Gram Panchayat (GP)* Zilla Parishad (ZP)* Nagar Panchayat (NP)* MunicipalityThe observations should be prepared for inclusion in official audit reports.Writing Style:* Use formal and objective audit language.* Write in passive voice.* Use indirect and reported speech.* Avoid personal opinions.* Mention facts based on audit findings.* Highlight control weaknesses.* Keep the observation concise but sufficiently detailed.Format:Title:Provide a short and specific title describing the audit issue.Body:Write one paragraph only.The paragraph should contain:1. Audit Finding:Mention the issue noticed during audit along with specific details such as:* Name of activity/project.* Period.* Amount involved.* Quantity.* Records examined.* Nature of irregularity.2. Impact:Explain the adverse effect of the finding, including:* Financial implications.* Weakness in internal controls.* Risk of misuse or loss of public funds.* Non-achievement of objectives.3. Recommendation:Provide corrective action in passive voice.The recommendation should mention:* Improvement of procedures.* Strengthening of controls.* Maintenance of proper records.* Compliance with applicable rules.Focus:Prepare observations that are suitable for Local Fund Audit Reports of Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies.Examples of areas:* Public works.* Procurement.* Tendering.* Contracts.* Grants.* Revenue collection.* Tax assessment.* Stores management.* Asset management.* Scheme implementation.* Financial records.* Cash management.* Advances and recoveries.Ensure every observation follows this structure:TitleOne paragraph containing:Finding → Impact → Recommendation Markdown Template for Audit Observation Library The following template can be used to create a GitHub Pages audit knowledge repository.
--- title: "Irregular Procurement of Materials" date: 2026-08-05 10:00:00 +0000 categories: [audit, procurement] tags: [local-fund-audit, procurement, irregularity, control-weakness] description: "Audit observation regarding procurement irregularities in local bodies." --- # Irregular Procurement of Materials During the audit of procurement activities of the Gram Panchayat, it was observed that materials amounting to ₹5.00 lakh were purchased without following prescribed procurement procedures and without maintaining adequate supporting documents. The irregular procurement process indicated weakness in internal controls and increased the risk of non-transparent expenditure, excessive payment, and improper utilization of public funds. It was recommended that all procurements be made after following prescribed procedures and that complete records including quotations, approvals, and utilization details be maintained for verification. --- ## Prompt Used Write an audit observation in the style of a Local Fund Auditor examining a Gram Panchayat, Zilla Parishad, Nagar Panchayat, or Municipality. The observation should: - Have a clear title. - Contain one paragraph. - Mention audit finding. - Explain impact. - Provide recommendation. - Use formal audit language. - Use passive voice. - Highlight control weaknesses. Possible Audit Observation Categories A structured audit repository can contain observations under the following categories:
Financial Management Examples:
Non-maintenance of cash book. Delay in bank reconciliation. Irregular advances. Non-recovery of dues. Procurement Audit Examples:
Purchase without quotation. Splitting of purchases. Non-compliance with tender rules. Excess payment to suppliers. Public Works Audit Examples:
Delay in completion. Defective execution. Excess measurement. Payment without verification. Asset Management Examples:
Non-maintenance of asset register. Idle assets. Missing inventory records. Lack of physical verification. Revenue Audit Examples:
Short collection of taxes. Non-revision of rates. Outstanding recoveries. Scheme Implementation Examples:
Diversion of funds. Non-utilization of grants. Missing beneficiary records. Benefits of a Standard Prompt-Based Audit System A structured prompt system helps in:
Preparing uniform audit observations. Reducing drafting time. Maintaining consistent audit language. Creating an audit observation database. Training new auditors. Building digital audit knowledge repositories. Developing AI-assisted audit documentation systems. Conclusion A well-designed audit observation format ensures that audit findings are communicated clearly and professionally. For Local Fund Audit institutions examining Gram Panchayats, Zilla Parishads, Nagar Panchayats, and Municipalities, maintaining a standardized observation structure improves report quality and strengthens accountability in local governance.
The combination of structured templates and reusable prompts can support creation of a searchable audit observation library for future audits.

GST Audit Explained: A Complete Beginner-to-Expert Guide Goods and Services Tax (GST) follows a self-assessment system, where every registered taxpayer is responsible for determining the correct tax liability, paying taxes on time, and filing accurate returns. Since the tax authorities do not verify every transaction before accepting returns, audits play a crucial role in ensuring compliance.
This guide explains the GST audit process from the basics to advanced concepts, covering internal audits, departmental audits, audit procedures, notices, observations, replies, and practical audit checklists.
What is GST Audit? A GST audit is the systematic examination of:
Books of accounts GST returns Tax invoices Financial statements Supporting documents The objective is to verify:
Correct turnover Correct tax payment Proper Input Tax Credit (ITC) Valid refund claims Compliance with GST law Objectives of GST Audit A GST audit aims to:
Verify correctness of GST returns. Detect under-reporting of turnover. Verify tax liability. Ensure correct ITC claims. Verify reverse charge liability. Check refund claims. Ensure statutory compliance. Prevent tax evasion. Types of GST Audit Type Legal Provision Conducted By Departmental Audit Section 65 GST Officer Special Audit Section 66 Chartered Accountant or Cost Accountant nominated by Commissioner Internal GST Audit Business Management Internal Auditor / Consultant Internal GST Audit vs Departmental GST Audit Aspect Internal Audit Departmental Audit Nature Voluntary Mandatory if selected Authority Conducted by business Conducted by GST Department Purpose Preventive Investigative Impact Helps avoid notices May result in demand or penalty Frequency Continuous Periodic Complete GST Audit Process Step 1 – Selection of Taxpayer A taxpayer may be selected based on:
High turnover Large ITC claims Large refund claims Multiple GST registrations Risk-based analytics Complaints Data mismatch Industry risk profile Previous non-compliance Step 2 – Issue of Audit Notice The GST department issues an audit notice (Form GST ADT-01 for departmental audits). The notice specifies:
Audit period Audit dates Officer details List of required records Place of audit Notice must generally be issued at least 15 working days before commencement of the audit.
Step 3 – Preparation by Taxpayer The taxpayer prepares all documents, including:
GSTR-1, GSTR-3B, and GSTR-9 Books of accounts (Trial Balance, P&L, Balance Sheet) Sales and Purchase Registers Stock and Fixed Asset Registers ITC Register and E-way Bills Bank Statements, Contracts, and Agreements Debit and Credit Notes Step 4 – Commencement of Audit Audit begins when records are submitted or when the audit actually starts at the business premises, whichever is later.
Step 5 – Examination of Records This is the core stage where every major compliance area is verified against statutory records.
Detailed GST Audit Checks 1. GST Registration Check Verify:
GSTIN details (Trade name, Legal name, Constitution) Declared business activities and HSN/SAC codes Additional places of business and amendments Relevant Forms: REG-01 (Application), REG-06 (Certificate), REG-14 (Amendment).
2. Return Filing Check Verify:
Timely filing and frequency Nil returns where applicable Payment of late fees and interest Important Returns:
GSTR-1: Invoice-wise outward supplies GSTR-3B: Monthly summary return (Tax liability, ITC, Tax payment) GSTR-9: Annual return GSTR-9C: Reconciliation statement (Books vs. Annual Return) 3. Sales Verification Reconcile turnover and tax calculation: Sales Register → GSTR-1 → GSTR-3B → Financial Statements
4. Purchase Verification Verify supplier authenticity, valid GSTIN, tax invoices, receipt of goods/services, and accounting entries.
5. Input Tax Credit (ITC) Compare: Purchase Register → GSTR-2B → GSTR-3B
Verify:
ITC claimed matches eligible documents. Goods/services were received. Supplier has reported invoices. Credit is not blocked under Section 17(5) (e.g., motor vehicles, club memberships, food/personal expenses). 6. Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM) Verify:
RCM liability identified Tax paid in cash ITC claimed correctly on eligible RCM payments 7. Turnover Verification Compare turnover declared across: Books → GSTR-1 → GSTR-3B → Annual Return → Income Tax Return
Check for unaccounted sales, duplicate reporting, or omitted invoices.
8. Tax Rate Verification Verify correct GST rates, tariff classifications, applicable notifications, and exemption eligibility.
9. Credit Notes and Debit Notes Verify proper issuance, correct reporting in returns, tax adjustments, and customer linkages.
10. Invoice Compliance Ensure every invoice contains: GSTINs, Invoice Number/Date, HSN/SAC, Description, Quantity, Taxable Value, Tax Rates (CGST/SGST/IGST), Place of Supply, and Authorized Signature.
11. E-Way Bill Verification Cross-verify required generation, vehicle numbers, invoice matching, quantity, value, destination, and distance. Mismatches may indicate unrecorded movement or fake invoicing.
12. 180-Day Payment Rule Reconcile: Invoice Date → Payment Date
If payment to the supplier exceeds 180 days from the invoice date, verify whether the corresponding ITC was reversed along with applicable interest.
13. Stock Verification Physically and documentary verify stock against Stock Registers, sales, purchases, wastage, job work, and finished goods.
14. Refund Verification Verify export documents, Shipping Bills, LUT/Bond declarations, Bank Realisation Certificates (BRC/FIRC), and refund calculations.
15. Financial Statement Reconciliation Reconcile balances between the Trial Balance, P&L, Balance Sheet, and GST Returns.
GST Audit Matrix Audit Area Documents Required Primary Verification Registration REG Forms GSTIN, Business Details Sales Sales Register Turnover & Rate Verification Purchases Purchase Register Genuine Receipt & Entry Returns GSTR-1, 3B, 9 Compliance & Timeliness ITC GSTR-2B, Invoices Eligibility & 180-day Rule RCM Books, Payment Vouchers Tax Paid in Cash Stock Stock Register Physical vs. Book Quantity E-way Bills EWB Portal Data Movement Matching Refund RFD Forms, BRC Export Eligibility Financials Balance Sheet, Trial Balance Reconciliation Audit Observations & Notices Audit Forms Summary ADT-01: Notice for commencement of departmental audit. ADT-02: Communication of audit findings after completion of departmental audit. ADT-03: Order for Special Audit (conducted by a nominated CA/CMA). ADT-04: Final report submitted by nominated auditor in Special Audit. How to Reply to Audit Observations Formulate replies using this structure:
Reference to notice / observation number Background of the transaction Detailed factual explanation Supporting documentary evidence Relevant statutory GST provisions/clarifications Formal request to drop the objection Possible Outcomes After Audit No Discrepancy: Audit closed via formal communication. Minor Discrepancy: Taxpayer pays tax/interest voluntarily; proceedings closed. Serious Discrepancy: Department issues Show Cause Notice (SCN) under Section 73 or 74 for demand and penalty recovery. Best Practices for Internal GST Audit Perform these routine monthly reconciliations:
Sales Register vs. GSTR-1 GSTR-1 vs. GSTR-3B Purchase Register vs. GSTR-2B Books vs. GST Returns E-way Bills vs. Invoices Trial Balance vs. GST Returns Final Thoughts A well-planned GST audit is more than a compliance exercise. It is an opportunity to identify process weaknesses, strengthen internal controls, improve documentation, and reduce future tax risks. Businesses that perform regular internal GST audits are better prepared for departmental scrutiny, respond more effectively to audit observations, and minimize the likelihood of penalties and litigation.
Whether you are a student, accountant, tax professional, auditor, or business owner, mastering GST audit requires understanding both the legal framework and the practical process of reconciliation, verification, documentation, and evidence-based reporting.

Point-wise Evidence-based Professional Legally supported Suggested structure:
Reference to notice Background Observation number Explanation Supporting documents Relevant GST provisions Request to drop objection Possible Outcomes After Audit Case 1 No discrepancy.
Audit closed.
Case 2 Minor discrepancy.
Taxpayer pays tax voluntarily.
Audit closed.
Case 3 Serious discrepancy.
Department issues:
Show Cause Notice Demand Notice Penalty proceedings where applicable Best Practices for Internal GST Audit Conduct these reconciliations every month:
Sales Register vs GSTR-1 GSTR-1 vs GSTR-3B Purchase Register vs GSTR-2B Books vs GST Returns E-way Bills vs Invoices ITC Register vs Purchase Register Trial Balance vs GST Returns Maintain:
Document checklist Audit working papers Reconciliation statements Management responses Compliance tracker Common Errors Found During GST Audit Excess ITC claim Wrong GST rate Missing invoices Duplicate invoices Incorrect HSN/SAC Incorrect Place of Supply RCM non-payment E-way bill mismatch Unreported turnover Late return filing Wrong refund claim Ineligible exemptions Beginner Learning Roadmap Stage 1 Learn:
GST basics Registration Tax invoice Returns Stage 2 Understand:
GSTR-1 GSTR-3B GSTR-2B ITC RCM Stage 3 Practice:
Return reconciliation Ledger verification Invoice verification ITC reconciliation Stage 4 Learn:
Departmental audit Special audit Notices Replies Demand proceedings Stage 5 Master:
Audit planning Working papers Risk assessment Financial statement reconciliation GST litigation support Audit reporting Final Thoughts A well-planned GST audit is more than a compliance exercise. It is an opportunity to identify process weaknesses, strengthen internal controls, improve documentation, and reduce future tax risks. Businesses that perform regular internal GST audits are better prepared for departmental scrutiny, respond more effectively to audit observations, and minimize the likelihood of penalties and litigation.
Whether you are a student, accountant, tax professional, auditor, or business owner, mastering GST audit requires understanding both the legal framework and the practical process of reconciliation, verification, documentation, and evidence-based reporting.

Automating GST Return PDF Audits with Python GST audits often involve reviewing hundreds of PDF returns downloaded from the GST portal. Manually copying tables or searching through lengthy documents is slow, repetitive, and prone to errors.
This guide demonstrates how to automate the process using two Python scripts:
pdf_to_csv.py – Extracts tables from GST return PDFs into CSV files. pdf_to_text.py – Extracts readable text and tables into structured text files. The scripts are designed for batch processing, making them useful for auditors, accountants, tax consultants, and finance professionals.
Why Automate GST PDF Processing? Most GST returns are distributed as PDF documents, including:
GSTR-1 GSTR-3B GSTR-9 GSTR-9C Electronic Cash Ledger Electronic Credit Ledger Liability Register An audit usually requires comparing reported values, reconciling invoices, verifying tax payments, identifying inconsistencies, and importing data into Excel. Automation significantly reduces manual effort.
Project Structure gst-pdf-tools/ ├── pdf_to_csv.py ├── pdf_to_text.py ├── sample1.pdf ├── sample2.pdf ├── csv_output/ │ ├── sample1.csv │ └── sample2.csv └── text_output/ ├── sample1.txt └── sample2.txt The scripts automatically create the output folders if they do not already exist.
Required Software Install the necessary Python packages:
pip install pandas pdfplumber tabula-py Since Tabula relies on Java, ensure Java is installed and verified on your system:
java -version Script 1: PDF to CSV (pdf_to_csv.py) This script extracts every detected table from every PDF in the working folder and saves it as a CSV.
import os import glob import tabula output_dir = "csv_output" os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True) pdf_files = glob.glob("*.pdf") for pdf_file in pdf_files: print(f"Processing {pdf_file}...") try: tables = tabula.read_pdf(pdf_file, pages="all", multiple_tables=True) if tables: # Combine all extracted tables from the file import pandas as pd combined_df = pd.concat(tables, ignore_index=True) base_name = os.path.splitext(pdf_file)[0] output_path = os.path.join(output_dir, f"{base_name}.csv") combined_df.to_csv(output_path, index=False) print(f"✓ Saved: {output_path}\n") else: print(f"No tables found in {pdf_file}. Skipping.\n") except Exception as e: print(f"Error processing {pdf_file}: {e}\n") Script 2: PDF to Text (pdf_to_text.py) The second script captures page text, headings, remarks, and tables for searching, indexing, or AI processing.
import os import glob import pdfplumber output_dir = "text_output" os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True) pdf_files = glob.glob("*.pdf") for pdf_file in pdf_files: print(f"Extracting text from {pdf_file}...") base_name = os.path.splitext(pdf_file)[0] output_path = os.path.join(output_dir, f"{base_name}.txt") try: with pdfplumber.open(pdf_file) as pdf, open(output_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as out_file: for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages, start=1): out_file.write(f"------------\nPage {i}\n------------\n\n") text = page.extract_text() if text: out_file.write(text + "\n\n") print(f"✓ Saved: {output_path}\n") except Exception as e: print(f"Error processing {pdf_file}: {e}\n") Sample Output Format Text Output Structure ------------ Page 1 ------------ GSTIN: 11ABCDE1234F1Z5 Legal Name: ABC Enterprises Return Period: April 2026 Table 1 Taxable Value 120000 CGST 10800 SGST 10800 CSV Output Structure GSTIN,Taxable Value,CGST,SGST,IGST 11ABCDE1234F1Z5,120000,10800,10800,0 Applications in GST Audit These scripts enable automation across multiple compliance tasks:
GSTR-3B Verification: Extract taxable turnover, output tax, ITC claimed, and tax paid directly into Excel. GSTR-1 Analysis: Extract invoice summaries to cross-check against sales registers and ERP exports. Annual Return Verification: Collect turnover, tax liability, and ITC adjustments automatically across multiple quarters. Ledger Review: Convert electronic credit and cash ledgers into searchable text files for easy anomaly detection. Audit Automation Pipeline Integrate these utilities into an end-to-end data processing pipeline:
Step 1: Download return PDFs from the GST Portal. Step 2: Run pdf_to_csv.py and pdf_to_text.py for batch extraction. Step 3: Load extracted CSVs into pandas or Power Query for automatic reconciliation. Step 4: Generate exception reports and audit observations. Git Integration Add the scripts to your GitHub repository to maintain version control:
git add pdf_to_csv.py pdf_to_text.py git commit -m "Add GST PDF processing scripts" git push origin main Best Practices Keep Source Data Intact: Store original PDFs in a read-only directory and output processed data separately. Validate Extraction: Perform sample checks on extracted CSVs against source PDFs before running large reconciliations. Batch by Period: Organize PDFs into folder structures by Financial Year or Month to streamline data merging. Conclusion Automating GST PDF processing eliminates repetitive data entry from audit workflows. By extracting structured CSVs and searchable text files, auditors can focus on analytical reviews, risk assessment, and reporting rather than manual transcriptions.

Building a Practical GST Compliance Audit Framework Over the course of this project, the goal was not simply to prepare another GST audit report. The objective was to build a repeatable audit methodology that can be used by government auditors, internal auditors, chartered accountants, and finance professionals for conducting GST compliance audits efficiently.
The work evolved from preparing simple audit observations into developing a structured audit framework, reusable templates, reconciliation tools, reporting formats, and workflow automation.
This article summarizes the complete journey.
Why This Project Started Many GST audits suffer from common problems:
Audit observations are inconsistent. Documentation is incomplete. Every auditor follows a different reporting style. Manual reconciliation consumes most of the audit time. Important red flags remain unnoticed. The idea was to create a standardized audit workflow that reduces manual effort while improving audit quality.
Understanding the Audit Process The audit was designed around one simple principle:
Everything must reconcile.
Every figure appearing in GST Returns should reconcile with:
Books of Accounts Purchase Register Sales Register Bank Statements E-Way Bills Financial Statements Whenever reconciliation fails, an audit observation is created.
Learning GST Audit in 24 Hours Instead of memorizing the CGST Act, the focus shifted toward high-impact practical auditing.
The audit process was divided into four major stages.
Stage 1 — Collect Data Essential documents include:
GSTR-1 GSTR-3B GSTR-2A GSTR-2B GSTR-9 Purchase Register Sales Register Trial Balance Ledger Bank Statements E-Way Bills Without these documents, meaningful verification cannot begin.
Stage 2 — Reconciliation Four reconciliations provide maximum audit value:
Sales: Books → Sales Register → GSTR-1 → GSTR-3B Purchases: Purchase Register → Books → GSTR-2B → ITC Claimed Banking: Bank Deposits → Sales → GST Returns Transportation: Purchase Invoices → Vehicle Numbers → E-Way Bills → Distance → Supervision Charges Templates Developed During the project several reusable templates were created.
GST Audit Checklist The checklist covers:
Registration GST Returns ITC Purchase Register Sales Register E-Way Bills Credit Notes HSN Codes Reverse Charge Bank Reconciliation Annual Returns Instead of relying on memory, auditors can simply follow the checklist.
GST Audit Report Format The report structure contains:
Executive Summary Audit Objectives Scope Methodology Detailed Audit Observations Risk Assessment Recommendations Conclusion This provides a uniform reporting format.
Client Information Sheet Basic information captured includes:
GSTIN Legal Name Trade Name Constitution Registration Date Business Nature Jurisdiction HSN Codes This becomes the first page of every audit.
Excel Tools Several Excel templates were designed.
GST Reconciliation Workbook Separate sheets were created for:
GSTR-1 GSTR-3B GSTR-2B Books Sales Books Purchase This structure allows Power Query to merge and compare records automatically.
Dashboard The dashboard displays:
Sales Difference Purchase Difference ITC Difference Tax Difference Status (Match / Mismatch) This instantly highlights risky areas.
Power Query Automation Instead of manually comparing thousands of invoices, Power Query can:
Import GST data Merge tables Compare invoices Flag differences Generate exception reports Typical workflow: Books Sales → Merge → GSTR-1 → Difference Column → Mismatch Report
The same process applies to purchases and ITC.
Professional Audit Observations One major improvement during the project was rewriting observations into professional audit language.
Instead of merely describing the issue, every observation now contains:
Observation Audit Criteria Risk Implication Recommendation This approach aligns with standard audit reporting practices.
Major Audit Observations The Balaji Enterprises audit produced several significant findings.
1. Non-maintenance of Purchase Register The entity produced GSTR-2A instead of the purchase register maintained in its books.
This violates:
Section 35 of CGST Act Rule 56 of CGST Rules Impact:
ITC cannot be verified. Purchases remain unsubstantiated. 2. Inadmissible Input Tax Credit ITC was claimed on:
iPhone Personal Tour Section 17(5)(g) specifically disallows ITC on personal consumption.
Recommended action:
Reverse ITC with applicable interest.
3. Missing Purchase Documentation Portal records indicated purchases from multiple suppliers.
However, only a small portion of invoices were produced.
This prevents verification of:
ITC Purchase authenticity Financial accuracy 4. Price Equalization Discounts The entity claimed price equalization through ledger entries.
No supporting credit notes were produced.
Without documentary evidence, discounts cannot be verified.
5. Sale Below Purchase Cost Cement was purchased at approximately ₹290 per bag.
Sale price averaged approximately ₹292.
Such thin margins deserve examination because they may indicate:
Undervaluation Price manipulation Artificial ITC accumulation 6. Sales Register vs GSTR-1 Differences existed between:
Taxable Value CGST SGST IGST These mismatches require reconciliation before the financial statements can be considered reliable.
7. Missing HSN Codes Only a limited number of HSN codes were declared.
However, audit found additional hardware items being traded.
Potential consequences include:
Wrong tax rate Incorrect invoice classification GST reporting inconsistencies Recommendation:
Update GST registration and ensure invoices reflect correct HSN codes.
8. Missing Sales Invoices Complete sales invoices were not produced.
This prevented:
Verification of turnover Sample testing Matching with GST returns 9. GSTR-9 Not Filed Annual return for one financial year remained unverified.
This increases compliance risk.
10. Income Tax Return Not Produced The entity claimed exemption.
No documentary evidence was produced.
11. Vehicle Number Repetition Identical vehicle numbers appeared across multiple invoices.
Further verification is required to rule out documentation errors.
12. E-Way Bill Issues Observed issues included:
Missing E-Way Bills Underreported distance Non-generation below threshold These require closer scrutiny.
13. Supervision Charges Goods transported between Siliguri and Gangtok frequently reflected only 10 km instead of the expected route distance.
If confirmed, this may affect computation of supervision charges.
The report recommends verification with supporting transport records before determining liability.
14. Bank Reconciliation Bank deposits substantially exceeded GST turnover in certain years.
Possible reasons include:
Unrecorded sales Timing differences Non-GST receipts Classification issues This area requires detailed reconciliation before any conclusion is drawn.
Risk Assessment Each observation was categorized based on severity.
Risk Examples High Wrong ITC, Sales Suppression, Missing Registers Medium HSN Issues, GSTR-9, Missing Credit Notes Low Documentation Improvements This helps management prioritize corrective action.
Documents Requested The audit also tracks document availability.
Examples include:
Purchase Register Sales Register Credit Notes Balance Sheet Profit & Loss Account Annual Report GST Returns E-Way Bills Maintaining a requisition tracker prevents repeated requests.
Final Recommendations The project resulted in a practical audit methodology.
Key recommendations include:
Maintain proper statutory books. Reconcile GST returns every month. Verify ITC only after GSTR-2B matching. Preserve supporting documents for discounts. Update HSN classifications regularly. Perform periodic internal GST reviews. Strengthen documentation before statutory audit. Tools Created During This Project The following resources were developed:
GST Audit Checklist GST Audit Report Template Excel Reconciliation Workbook Power Query Reconciliation Workflow Dashboard Template Client Data Collection Format Observation Templates Meeting Record Format Risk Assessment Matrix Recommendation Tracker These templates can be adapted for future GST audits with minimal modification.
Lessons Learned The biggest lesson from this project is that GST auditing is less about memorizing legal provisions and more about systematic verification.
A disciplined workflow built around reconciliation, documentation, and evidence allows auditors to identify most compliance issues efficiently.
Standardized templates, automation with Excel and Power Query, and well-structured audit observations significantly reduce audit effort while improving consistency and report quality.
For audit teams, investing time in reusable tools pays dividends across every future engagement.

Building a Python Toolkit for GST Return PDF Auditing GST return PDFs contain valuable information for auditors, but extracting that information manually is slow, repetitive, and error-prone. This project documents the process of building an open-source Python toolkit that converts GST return PDFs into structured data suitable for audit analysis.
The goal is to create a reusable toolkit that can process hundreds of GST returns with minimal manual effort.
Project Objectives The toolkit should be able to:
Process multiple GST PDF files automatically Extract tables into CSV files Extract text into structured text files Preserve page structure Handle complex GST tables Produce outputs suitable for Excel, Power BI, Pandas, and SQL Be easy to use from the command line Be hosted on GitHub Understanding GST Return PDFs GST returns are generated in several formats including:
GSTR-1 GSTR-2A GSTR-2B GSTR-3B GSTR-9 GSTR-9C These PDFs generally contain:
GSTIN Legal Name Return Period Invoice Details HSN Summary Taxable Value CGST SGST IGST Cess Place of Supply Tax Paid ITC Claimed Most GST PDFs contain:
Multi-line cells Split tables Repeated headers Nested tables Rotated pages Mixed text and tables These characteristics make extraction challenging.
Choosing the Right PDF Libraries Initially, the project used:
tabula-py pdfplumber These work well for many GST reports but struggle with highly formatted documents.
After evaluating several libraries, a better toolkit emerged.
Library Purpose Rating pdfplumber Text extraction ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Camelot Table extraction ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ PyMuPDF Fast page reading ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ pdfminer.six Low-level text extraction ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Tabula Simple table extraction ⭐⭐⭐⭐ OCR (Tesseract) Scanned PDFs ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ The toolkit can later combine these libraries to maximize extraction accuracy.
First Utility: PDF to CSV The first utility scans the current folder for every PDF.
Example:
invoice1.pdfinvoice2.pdfgstr3b.pdf It automatically generates:
csv_output/invoice1.csvinvoice2.csvgstr3b.csv Main features include:
Batch processing Automatic output folder creation Error handling Empty table detection Logging UTF-8 compatibility Second Utility: PDF to Structured Text CSV extraction works well for tables.
However, GST PDFs also contain:
Headings Notes Return summaries Footer information Legal declarations The second utility extracts:
Page-wise text Tables Page separators Structured output Example output:
---------------------------------Page 1---------------------------------GSTIN11ABCDE1234F1Z5Return PeriodApril 2025---------------------------------TableInvoice No Date TaxableINV001 ... This structured format is ideal for:
LLMs RAG systems Search engines Audit evidence Repository Structure The project was organized into a clean GitHub repository.
gst-pdf-audit-tools/│├── pdf_to_csv.py├── pdf_to_text.py├── requirements.txt├── README.md│├── csv_output/│├── text_output/│└── .github/└── workflows/python-test.yml Keeping outputs separate from source code simplifies maintenance.
Dependency Management A simple requirements.txt was created.
camelot-py[cv]pdfplumberPyMuPDFpdfminer.sixpandasopenpyxltabulate Installation:
pip install -r requirements.txt Windows Installation Warnings During installation, Windows displayed warnings similar to:
WARNING:The script camelot.exe is installed in ...which is not on PATH. These warnings are not installation failures.
They simply indicate that executable scripts are installed in a directory that Windows cannot access from the command prompt.
Python libraries continue to function normally when imported.
Adding the Scripts directory to the Windows PATH removes these warnings for future command-line use.
Why Camelot Is Better Than Tabula Both libraries extract tables.
However, Camelot offers several advantages.
Stream Mode Useful for tables without borders.
camelot.read_pdf( pdf, flavor="stream" ) Lattice Mode Useful when PDFs have visible grid lines.
camelot.read_pdf( pdf, flavor="lattice" ) Accuracy Metrics Camelot reports:
Accuracy Whitespace Parsing quality This allows automatic rejection of poor-quality tables.
Why pdfplumber Is Excellent pdfplumber provides:
Character-level extraction Word coordinates Table detection Image positions Bounding boxes This makes it valuable for GST reports where layouts vary significantly.
Future Improvements The toolkit can evolve into a comprehensive GST audit platform.
Possible enhancements include:
Data Cleaning Automatically remove:
Blank rows Duplicate headers Empty columns GST Validation Validate:
GSTIN format Invoice numbers HSN codes Dates Tax Recalculation Automatically compute:
CGST SGST IGST and compare with reported values.
Cross Verification Compare:
GSTR-1 GSTR-3B GSTR-2B Books of Accounts to identify mismatches.
Audit Flags Generate observations such as:
Missing invoices Duplicate invoices Incorrect tax rates ITC mismatches Negative taxable values Invalid GSTINs Export Formats Support additional outputs:
CSV Excel SQLite JSON Markdown OCR Support Many GST returns are scanned.
Integrating:
Tesseract OCR OCRmyPDF would allow extraction from scanned documents.
GitHub Automation GitHub Actions can automatically:
Check Python syntax Install dependencies Run unit tests Build documentation Publish releases This keeps the repository reliable for contributors.
Long-Term Vision The toolkit is intended to become a complete GST audit automation framework.
Future modules may include:
PDF ingestion OCR preprocessing Table extraction Data normalization GSTIN validation HSN validation Return reconciliation Risk scoring Exception reporting Dashboard generation AI-assisted audit observations Ultimately, auditors should be able to place hundreds of GST return PDFs into a folder and receive clean, structured datasets along with exception reports that significantly reduce manual effort.
Conclusion Processing GST return PDFs is one of the most time-consuming aspects of GST auditing. By combining modern Python libraries such as Camelot, pdfplumber, PyMuPDF, and pandas, it is possible to automate much of this work.
A well-designed toolkit not only saves time but also improves consistency, enables large-scale analysis, and provides a strong foundation for advanced audit analytics, reconciliation, and AI-assisted compliance review.

Building an Audit Report Analysis System with GitHub Pages Managing hundreds of audit reports becomes increasingly difficult as the number of local bodies, audit years, and observations grows. Traditional document storage makes searching, comparing, and analyzing reports time-consuming.
This project aims to transform audit reports into a searchable knowledge base using GitHub Pages, GitHub Actions, JavaScript, and a small amount of Python.
The result is a completely free system that automatically converts reports, builds an index, and provides an interactive website for browsing audit reports.
Project Goals The objectives are:
Store audit reports in a GitHub repository Automatically convert DOCX and PDF reports into Markdown Generate metadata for every report Build a searchable website Allow future statistical analysis Keep hosting completely free using GitHub Pages Overall Architecture Audit Report│▼DOCX / PDF│▼GitHub Repository│▼GitHub Actions│▼Python Conversion│├── Markdown Files├── JSON Database└── Statistics│▼GitHub Pages│▼Interactive Website Why GitHub Pages? GitHub Pages offers several advantages.
Completely free No server maintenance Automatic deployment Excellent version control Easy collaboration Fast global CDN The limitation is that GitHub Pages only serves static files.
There is no backend.
Therefore, document conversion must happen before deployment.
Why Use Markdown? Markdown is an excellent storage format for audit reports.
Example:
# Audit Report ## Observation 1 Improper maintenance of cash book. ## Observation 2 Utilization certificates not submitted. Advantages include:
Human readable Git friendly Small file size Easy searching Easy rendering Works directly with GitHub Pages Markdown vs JSON vs XML Markdown Best for reading.
Example:
## Observation 12 Stock Register not maintained. Advantages
Very readable Git diff friendly Easy editing Works with Markdown renderers Disadvantages
Harder to perform analytics JSON Best for applications.
Example
{ "unit":"Gangtok Municipal Corporation", "year":2025, "observations":24 } Advantages
Fast searching Structured Easy filtering Great for dashboards Disadvantages
Not pleasant to read manually XML Mostly useful when exchanging data between software.
Example
<report> <unit>Gangtok</unit> </report> Advantages
Standardized Validation support Disadvantages
Verbose Difficult to read Rarely needed for this project Recommended Storage Strategy Store both formats.
report.mdreport.json Markdown is for reading.
JSON is for searching and analytics.
Why Not Use Only JavaScript? Initially it seems possible.
Unfortunately browsers cannot reliably convert DOCX and PDF.
They have several limitations.
JavaScript Can Read Markdown Read JSON Search data Render reports Create dashboards Export CSV Filter reports JavaScript Cannot Reliably Parse complicated PDFs Preserve Word formatting Extract tables accurately Read scanned PDFs Perform OCR That is why preprocessing is required.
Hybrid Workflow The recommended workflow is:
Python↓Convert documents↓Markdown + JSON↓GitHub Repository↓GitHub Pages↓JavaScript Viewer Python runs only during preprocessing.
The website itself contains no Python.
Repository Structure audit-report-viewer/.github/workflows/css/js/data/database/templates/input/output/docs/README.mdLICENSEindex.htmlfiles.jsonlocalbodies.csv Everything remains organized.
Processing Workflow Upload↓DOCX/PDF↓Python↓Extract Text↓Identify Unit↓Identify Audit Year↓Count Observations↓Normalize Unit↓Generate Markdown↓Generate JSON↓Generate files.json↓GitHub Pages Observation Detection Every report contains audit observations.
Typical headings include:
Audit Findings Observation Audit Para Para Irregularities Compliance Issues The converter counts these automatically.
Example
Observation 1Observation 2Observation 3 Result
Observation Count = 3 Standardizing Local Body Names Different reports often use different spellings.
Example
Gangtok Municipal CouncilGangtok MCGMCGangtok Municipality All should become
Gangtok Municipal Corporation This is achieved using
localbodies.csv Example
Variant Standard GMC Gangtok Municipal Corporation Gangtok MC Gangtok Municipal Corporation Automatic File Naming Each converted report is renamed.
gangtok-municipal-corporation-2025-18.md Format
Unit-Year-ObservationCount Advantages
Easy sorting Easy searching Unique filenames Metadata Database Each report also generates JSON metadata.
Example
{ "unit_name":"Gangtok Municipal Corporation", "audit_year":2025, "observations":18, "filename":"gangtok-2025-18.md" } These entries become
files.json Why Dynamic files.json? Instead of maintaining JavaScript arrays manually:
const files = [...] GitHub Actions generates
files.json JavaScript simply fetches it.
fetch("files.json") Advantages
No manual updates Automatically synchronized Easier maintenance GitHub Actions Whenever new reports are uploaded:
Push↓Workflow↓Python↓Markdown↓JSON↓Commit↓GitHub Pages Updated Everything is automatic.
Website Features The frontend includes:
Search Filters Sort by year Sort by unit Markdown preview Responsive layout Floating navigation Error handling No backend required.
Search Features Users can search by
Unit Year Observation count Keywords Instant filtering occurs in the browser.
Sorting Reports can be sorted by
Audit Year Unit Name Observation Count Future additions include
District Department Risk Level Markdown Rendering Instead of showing raw Markdown
# Heading The site renders
Heading using marked.js.
Reports become pleasant to read.
Future Dashboard Ideas Once metadata exists, dashboards become straightforward.
Examples include
Reports by Year Reports by District Observation Trends High Risk Departments Observation Frequency Compliance Percentage Libraries
Chart.js Apache ECharts D3.js Error Handling The application should gracefully handle:
Missing reports Corrupted PDFs Duplicate filenames Invalid years Unknown local bodies Rather than crashing.
Documentation The repository should include
README CONTRIBUTING LICENSE Issue Templates Pull Request Templates This encourages collaboration.
Why GitHub Actions Instead of Running Python Locally? Advantages
Fully automated Consistent environment No manual steps Always up to date Easy collaboration Only uploading reports is required.
Everything else happens automatically.
Technologies Used Technology Purpose HTML Website CSS Styling JavaScript Frontend GitHub Pages Hosting GitHub Actions Automation Python Document conversion Markdown Report storage JSON Metadata Marked.js Markdown rendering PyMuPDF PDF extraction python-docx DOCX extraction Future Roadmap Phase 1 Convert reports Generate Markdown Generate JSON Phase 2 Search Filters Sorting Responsive interface Phase 3 Dashboards Statistics Observation categorization Phase 4 AI-assisted observation summarization Similar observation detection Duplicate observation identification Recommendation generation Trend analysis across years Final Thoughts This architecture combines the strengths of static hosting and automated preprocessing.
Python is used only where it excels—extracting structured information from DOCX and PDF documents. Once preprocessing is complete, GitHub Pages serves a fast, secure, and maintenance-free website powered entirely by HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
The approach keeps infrastructure simple while remaining scalable enough to manage thousands of audit reports, making it a practical long-term solution for creating a searchable digital audit archive and enabling future analytical capabilities such as dashboards, trend analysis, and AI-assisted insights.

Drafting Office Notings and Official Letters for Submission of the Annual Consolidated Audit Report Government correspondence demands clarity, precision, and compliance with statutory provisions. One such important communication is the submission of the Annual Consolidated Audit Report (ACAR) to the State Legislature.
Under the Sikkim Local Fund Audit Act, 2012, the Directorate of Local Fund Audit is required to prepare and submit the Annual Consolidated Audit Report for laying before the State Legislature. This process generally involves preparing an office noting seeking approval, forwarding authenticated and printed copies to the Legislative Assembly Secretariat, and uploading electronic copies wherever prescribed.
This article explains the purpose of these documents and provides model drafts that may be adapted for official use.
Legal Background Section 19 of the Sikkim Local Fund Audit Act, 2012 provides that the Annual Consolidated Audit Report shall be submitted to the Government for laying before the State Legislature.
Before every Assembly Session, the Legislative Assembly Secretariat generally communicates the schedule for the forthcoming session and requests submission of reports required to be laid before the House.
For the report relating to the financial year 2023–24, the Secretariat informed that the Assembly had been convened on 30 June 2025 vide Letter No. 411/L&PA/SLAS dated 18.06.2025.
Accordingly, the following documents were required to be submitted:
Two authenticated copies of the Annual Consolidated Audit Report. Forty printed copies. Soft copies in PDF and DOC formats uploaded online. Purpose of the Office Noting The office noting serves multiple purposes:
Records the statutory requirement. Refers to the communication received from the Legislative Assembly Secretariat. Indicates the documents prepared for submission. Seeks approval from the competent authority before dispatch. A well-drafted noting should be concise, factual, and avoid unnecessary narration.
Model Office Noting Subject Submission of Annual Consolidated Audit Report for the year ended 2023–24 to the Sikkim Legislative Assembly
It is submitted that, under the provisions of Section 19 of the Sikkim Local Fund Audit Act, 2012, the Annual Consolidated Audit Report for the year ended 2023–24 is required to be laid before the State Legislature.
In this connection, the Sikkim Legislative Assembly Secretariat, vide Letter No. 411/L&PA/SLAS dated 18.06.2025, has informed that the Assembly has been convened on 30 June 2025.
Accordingly, the following documents have been prepared for submission:

Soft copies of the report in PDF and DOC formats for uploading on the designated online portal. Approval is solicited to forward the authenticated copies, printed copies, and upload the electronic versions for submission to the Sikkim Legislative Assembly Secretariat for laying before the Legislature.
Submitted please.
Accounts Officer
Why Two Authenticated Copies? Authenticated copies are officially signed and certified copies of the report.
These copies serve as the official record maintained by the Legislative Assembly Secretariat and other designated authorities.
Why Forty Printed Copies? Printed copies are generally supplied for:
Hon’ble Speaker Hon’ble Members of the Legislative Assembly Legislative Assembly Secretariat Parliamentary Branch Record Sections Government Departments concerned The exact number depends upon the directions issued by the Secretariat.
Importance of Soft Copies Most legislatures now maintain digital repositories of reports.
Soft copies in both PDF and Word (DOC) formats enable:
Electronic record management. Online publication where permitted. Easy archival. Searchability. Future reference. Model Forwarding Letter No. ________/DLFA/ACAR/2025

Directorate of Local Fund Audit

Date: __________
To The Secretary,

DOC uploaded. Acknowledgement requested. Dispatch entered in the register. Best Practices for Government Drafting When preparing office notings and forwarding letters:
Quote the relevant statutory provision accurately. Mention the Assembly communication with its letter number and date. Clearly specify the number of copies enclosed. Mention electronic submission separately. End the office noting with “Submitted please.” Request acknowledgement in the forwarding letter. Maintain concise and formal language. Conclusion Submission of the Annual Consolidated Audit Report is a statutory responsibility that supports legislative oversight of local bodies. Proper documentation through an office noting and a formal forwarding letter ensures procedural compliance, accountability, and timely placement of the report before the Legislature.
Using standardized formats also improves consistency in government correspondence and facilitates efficient record management.

RTI Online Portal Training at NIC Sikkim On 25 June 2025, officials from various government departments attended a training programme conducted by the National Informatics Centre (NIC), Sikkim on the implementation and use of the RTI Online Portal.
The session focused on the complete lifecycle of an RTI application, user roles, workflow management, role assignment, and the responsibilities of various officers under the Right to Information Act.
This article summarizes the training and serves as a reference guide for future users of the RTI Online Portal.
Objectives of the Training The training was designed to help government officials:
Understand the RTI Online Portal. Learn the workflow for processing RTI applications. Understand the responsibilities of different users. Learn how applications are assigned and processed. Familiarize themselves with role-based access control. Ensure compliance with the guidelines issued by the Central Information Commission (CIC) and the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT). About the RTI Online Portal The RTI Online Portal enables citizens to submit RTI applications electronically and allows government departments to process those applications digitally.
The platform has been developed by NIC following the guidelines prescribed by:
Central Information Commission (CIC) Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) The system replaces much of the manual paperwork with an organized digital workflow.
Training Environment During the demonstration, the trainers used a test environment for practice.
Test Server [http://164.100.244.13](http://164.100.244.13) Demo OTP 111111 Note
The above server and OTP were used only for training purposes.
User Roles in the RTI Portal The portal uses a role-based access system.
Each user receives permissions according to their assigned role.
The major roles discussed during the training were:
Nodal SPIO SPIO ASPIO First Appellate Authority Consultant (if applicable) Understanding the Nodal SPIO One of the SPIOs in the department is designated as the Nodal SPIO.
This is one of the most important roles in the portal.
The Nodal SPIO acts as the administrator for the department.
Their responsibilities include:
Managing RTI users Assigning applications Creating workflow Assigning roles Monitoring RTI cases Responsibilities of the Nodal SPIO The Nodal SPIO can:
Assign RTI applications. Register users. Assign roles. Change user roles. Allocate applications to concerned SPIOs. Allocate work to ASPIOs. Configure departmental workflow. Only the Nodal SPIO has these administrative privileges.
Login Process During the first login:
Username is provided by the administrator. Password is sent through email. Users are required to change the password after the first login. This ensures secure access to the RTI portal.
Role Assignment One of the major topics covered during the training was role assignment.
Only the Nodal SPIO can assign roles.
Roles that can be assigned include:
SPIO ASPIO First Appellate Authority Consultant Other authorized users Ordinary users cannot change or assign roles.
RTI Application Workflow The portal follows a structured workflow.
Citizen │ ▼ RTI Application Submitted │ ▼ Nodal SPIO │ ▼ Assigns Application │ ▼ SPIO / ASPIO │ ▼ Prepare Reply │ ▼ SPIO Reviews │ ▼ Reply Sent to Applicant This ensures accountability and transparency.
Assigning RTI Tasks Whenever a new RTI application is received:
The application reaches the department. The Nodal SPIO reviews it. The application is assigned to the appropriate SPIO or ASPIO. The assigned officer processes the request. A reply is prepared. The portal keeps track of every stage.
Processing an RTI Application The training demonstrated several actions available to SPIOs.
These include:
Accept Application Forward Application Reject Application (where applicable) Each action is recorded within the portal.
Important Difference Between SPIO and ASPIO One of the most important concepts discussed during the session was the distinction between the SPIO and ASPIO.
ASPIO The ASPIO can:
Examine the RTI application. Collect information. Draft a reply. However:
The ASPIO cannot send the reply directly to the applicant.
SPIO The SPIO has the authority to:
Review the draft reply. Approve it. Send the final response to the applicant. Therefore, every reply prepared by an ASPIO must first reach the SPIO.
Only after approval can it be dispatched.
Why Only SPIO Can Send Replies This workflow ensures:
Proper accountability. Legal compliance. Departmental approval. Consistent communication. Official responsibility under the RTI Act. The SPIO remains legally responsible for the information supplied.
Security Features The portal includes several security measures.
These include:
User authentication Password-based login Email verification Role-based permissions Controlled workflow Audit trail These features reduce unauthorized access and improve transparency.
Advantages of the RTI Online Portal The online portal offers several advantages.
Faster Processing Applications move electronically without physical files.
Better Tracking Every application has a digital trail.
Transparency Each action is recorded.
Accountability Every officer performs actions according to assigned permissions.
Reduced Paperwork Digital processing minimizes manual handling.
Best Practices for Officers During the training, officers were advised to:
Check the portal regularly. Respond within prescribed timelines. Forward applications promptly. Maintain confidentiality. Upload accurate information. Review replies carefully before submission. Follow RTI Act provisions strictly. Common Workflow Example Suppose a citizen submits an RTI application.
The process would be:
Citizen submits the RTI online. Department receives the application. Nodal SPIO assigns it. ASPIO gathers information. ASPIO prepares the draft reply. SPIO reviews the draft. SPIO sends the reply. Applicant receives the official response. Key Takeaways The training emphasized several important points:
The RTI portal is fully role-based. The Nodal SPIO manages users and assignments. ASPIOs assist in processing applications. Only SPIOs can issue official replies. Every action is digitally recorded. The platform follows CIC and DoPT guidelines. Proper workflow improves transparency and accountability. Support Contacts RTI Portal Support Savita
Mobile: 9800013330
For technical issues related to the RTI Online Portal.
Departmental Nodal Officer Palden Thakunge
Directorate of Local Fund Audit
Email: sikkimlfa@gmail.com
Mobile: 9064283977
For departmental coordination and RTI implementation support.
Final Thoughts The RTI Online Portal represents a significant step toward transparent and efficient governance. By digitizing the entire RTI process, departments can process applications more efficiently while maintaining accountability at every stage.
Understanding the responsibilities of the Nodal SPIO, SPIO, and ASPIO is essential for ensuring timely responses and compliance with the Right to Information Act. Regular training and adherence to the prescribed workflow will help departments provide better public service and strengthen citizens’ trust in government institutions.

Training on Auditing Serious Irregularities (TGS): Key Lessons from the AG Office On 26 June 2025, officials from the Accountant General (AG) Office conducted a training-cum-discussion on Serious Irregularities (TGS). The session focused on strengthening the ability of auditors to identify, investigate, document, and report irregularities that have significant financial, legal, or governance implications.
The discussion emphasized that auditors should move beyond routine compliance checking and adopt a risk-based approach to detect irregularities that may involve fraud, corruption, deliberate misrepresentation, or systemic failures.
Why Serious Irregularities Matter Not every audit observation qualifies as a serious irregularity.
A serious irregularity generally involves one or more of the following:
Fraud or corruption Deliberate concealment of facts Misappropriation of government funds Financial loss to the Government Abuse of official position Non-compliance resulting in significant consequences Systemic weaknesses affecting governance Such cases require prompt reporting because they may lead to:
Departmental proceedings Criminal investigations Recovery of government money Forensic examination Policy reforms Objectives of the Training The session aimed to help auditors:
Understand what constitutes a serious irregularity. Learn methods for identifying high-risk transactions. Design suitable audit procedures. Improve documentation and evidence collection. Understand reporting protocols. Appreciate the role of forensic audit. Recommend corrective and preventive measures. Characteristics of Serious Irregularities The resource persons explained that serious irregularities generally involve one or more of the following characteristics.
1. Lack of Transparency Transactions intentionally kept outside established procedures.
Examples include:
Non-maintenance of records Concealment of documents Missing approvals Absence of supporting evidence 2. Deliberate Misrepresentation This involves knowingly presenting false information.
Examples include:
Inflated expenditure Under-reporting revenue False utilisation certificates Manipulation of financial statements Unlike ordinary errors, deliberate misrepresentation is intentional.
3. Use of Fake Documents Fake or fabricated documents are common indicators of fraud.
Examples discussed included:
Fake Aadhaar cards Forged certificates Fabricated vouchers False identity documents Altered invoices 4. Financial Fraud Financial fraud often involves illegal gain through misuse of government resources.
Examples discussed included:
Fraudulent Kisan Credit Card transactions Fake beneficiaries Unauthorized withdrawals Diversion of funds Examples Discussed During the Session Several practical examples were used to explain how serious irregularities arise.
Fraudulent Financial Transactions Examples included:
Employees obtaining financial benefits using fake documents. Fraudulent claims under government schemes. Misuse of subsidies. Procurement Irregularities The session highlighted common procurement issues such as:
No Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) Quotations obtained from preferred vendors only Conflict of interest Splitting of purchases Violation of procurement rules Such practices reduce transparency and increase the risk of corruption.
Mismanagement of Revenue One example involved departments failing to implement provisions of Acts or Rules that could generate government revenue.
Illustrations included:
Failure to collect irrigation tax. Failure to enforce revenue provisions. Weak monitoring mechanisms. Bypassing Administrative Procedures Examples included:
Junior officials directly approaching higher authorities. Ignoring prescribed approval hierarchy. Unauthorized decision-making. Such deviations weaken internal controls.
Seven Key Steps in Handling Serious Irregularities The training presented a structured framework.
Step 1: Identification The first responsibility of an auditor is to identify indicators of serious irregularities.
Possible red flags include:
Unusual transactions Missing files Fake documents Large cash payments Unsupported expenditure Sudden increase in expenditure Repeated payments to the same vendor Large-value transactions should receive greater scrutiny.
Random verification should also be performed.
Step 2: Design Appropriate Audit Procedures Once risk areas are identified, audit procedures should be tailored accordingly.
Possible procedures include:
Detailed scrutiny Third-party confirmation Bank reconciliation Physical verification Verification of approvals Review of electronic records Cross-checking departmental databases The emphasis should always be on obtaining sufficient and appropriate audit evidence.
Step 3: Reporting Timely reporting is critical.
Depending upon the seriousness, the matter may require reporting to:
Head of Office Finance Department Administrative Department Accountant General Vigilance Authorities Police authorities (where criminal offences are suspected) The training stressed that auditors should report facts supported by evidence and avoid speculative conclusions.
Step 4: Special Audit Certain cases require specialized examination.
Special audits may involve:
Experts Technical specialists Chartered accountants Departmental specialists The objective is to determine the complete extent of irregularity.
Step 5: Impact Assessment The consequences of serious irregularities extend beyond monetary loss.
Possible impacts include:
Financial Impact Loss of government revenue Wasteful expenditure Inadmissible payments Legal Impact Criminal prosecution Departmental action Recovery proceedings Institutional Impact Loss of public confidence Damage to departmental reputation Weak governance The training also referred to situations where funding agencies may impose penalties if serious financial irregularities are established.
Step 6: Forensic Audit Where fraud is suspected, forensic audit becomes essential.
Unlike routine audit, forensic audit focuses on evidence that can withstand legal scrutiny.
Important evidence includes:
Original files Note sheets Official correspondence Digital records Geo-tagged photographs Audio recordings Video recordings System logs Bank records Proper preservation of evidence is extremely important.
Step 7: Follow-Up Audit does not end with reporting.
Effective follow-up includes:
Corrective action Recovery of funds Strengthening internal controls Departmental proceedings Suspension where necessary Policy improvements Monitoring compliance The ultimate objective is preventing recurrence.
Importance of Risk Assessment Risk assessment should drive the audit process.
Auditors should identify:
High-risk departments High-value schemes Weak internal controls Revenue-sensitive functions Procurement-intensive activities A risk-based audit improves efficiency and increases the likelihood of detecting serious irregularities.
Internal Controls The training emphasized that effective internal controls reduce opportunities for fraud.
Important controls include:
Proper segregation of duties Bank reconciliation Periodic verification Approval hierarchy Handover procedures Asset verification Access controls Auditors should evaluate whether these controls are:
Adequate Functioning properly Regularly monitored Principles of Compliance Audit Reference was made to the principles governing compliance audit.
The discussion highlighted the following audit principles.
Legality All actions should comply with:
Acts Rules Government Orders Notifications Circulars Adequacy Internal control systems should be sufficient to safeguard public resources.
Transparency Government decisions should be transparent.
Records should be:
Properly maintained Easily traceable Fully documented Propriety and Prudence Auditors should also assess whether expenditure demonstrates:
Financial wisdom Economy Good governance Public interest Even if expenditure is technically legal, it may still violate the principles of propriety.
Effectiveness Government spending should produce intended outcomes.
Questions an auditor should ask include:
Were objectives achieved? Were resources used efficiently? Was public money spent economically? Were expected benefits delivered? Common Categories of Serious Irregularities The session broadly classified serious irregularities into the following groups.
1. Fraud and Corruption Examples:
Embezzlement Bribery Fake claims Misappropriation Deliberate falsification 2. Non-Compliance Examples:
Procurement violations Absence of NIT Ignoring prescribed procedures Tax evasion Conflict of interest 3. Mismanagement of Funds Examples:
Idle funds Diversion of funds Failure to generate revenue Poor financial management 4. Deviation from Established Procedures Examples:
Bypassing approval hierarchy Unauthorized sanctions Ignoring financial rules Weak administrative controls Reporting Serious Irregularities The resource persons emphasized that reports should be:
Objective Evidence-based Clear Concise Free from assumptions Auditors should avoid using words such as fraud or corruption unless supported by sufficient evidence.
Where evidence is still being developed, it is safer to describe the issue as a serious irregularity, supported by factual observations.
Value Addition by the AG Office The training concluded by explaining that reports submitted by Local Fund Audit offices are further examined by the AG Office.
The AG Office provides:
Technical guidance Additional scrutiny Quality assurance Value addition to audit findings Recommendations for further investigation where necessary This collaborative approach strengthens audit quality and improves accountability.
Key Takeaways The session reinforced several important lessons.
Serious irregularities require immediate attention. Risk assessment should guide audit planning. Strong evidence is the foundation of every audit finding. Documentation should be complete and reliable. Internal controls must be evaluated continuously. Follow-up is as important as detection. Professional judgment and objectivity are essential throughout the audit process. Final Thoughts Auditing serious irregularities is one of the most demanding responsibilities of a public sector auditor. Detecting such cases requires more than checking vouchers and registers. It demands analytical thinking, professional skepticism, careful documentation, and a thorough understanding of governance systems.
The training provided valuable practical insights into identifying red flags, designing appropriate audit procedures, collecting legally sustainable evidence, and ensuring that audit findings contribute to stronger financial management and public accountability.
For auditors working in Local Fund Audit and related organizations, these principles form the foundation of effective compliance auditing and help safeguard public resources through timely detection and reporting of serious irregularities.
