Internal auditing in government departments and public institutions is undergoing a fundamental shift. The traditional approach—checking 100% of vouchers, invoices, and ledger entries—is no longer feasible or effective in complex operational environments. Modern public financial oversight demands a move toward Risk-Based Internal Audit (RBIA).
By aligning audit coverage with organizational risk, auditors can focus their time and resources where material misstatements, systemic control failures, and non-compliance are most likely to occur.
This guide brings together the core principles of RBIA, the Audit Risk Model, practical planning strategies, and a breakdown of the 21 most common financial and compliance errors found during government internal audits.
1. Traditional Internal Audit vs. Risk-Based Internal Audit Traditional internal auditing is transaction-based. It focuses heavily on checking compliance for individual transactions after they occur. While useful for verifying mathematical accuracy, it often misses larger, systemic vulnerabilities.
In contrast, Risk-Based Internal Audit (RBIA) is a forward-looking methodology. It divides an entity into distinct business units or operational areas, assesses the inherent risks within each, and evaluates how effectively management mitigates those risks.
Key Distinctions Feature External Audit Traditional Internal Audit Risk-Based Internal Audit (RBIA) Primary Audience Shareholders & External Bodies Management & Board Management, Board & Governance Primary Focus Financial Statement Accuracy Transactional Compliance Risk Identification & System Assurance Methodology Standard Financial Sampling Checklist / Voucher Checking Risk Prioritization & Evaluation Resource Allocation Fixed Scope Universal / Uniform Coverage Targeted at High-Risk Units 2. The Core Categories of Operational Risk Under the RBIA framework, risks are categorized into four main domains. Categorization allows audit teams to evaluate both financial and non-financial threats to an organization’s objectives.
Strategic Risk: Threats that prevent an entity from achieving high-level goals aligned with its mission (e.g., policy changes, structural delays, external socioeconomic factors). Operational Risk: Risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, human error, system failures, or external disruptions to daily workflow. Reporting Risk: The probability that financial or performance reports contain material errors, omissions, or misleading information. Compliance Risk: Exposure to legal penalties, financial recovery orders, or severe reputational damage resulting from non-compliance with statutory rules, service regulations, or financial frameworks. Risk Prioritization Matrix (1 to 5 Scale) Auditors prioritize risk based on potential impact and likelihood using a standard 5-point scale:
Low: Negligible impact on operations or finances. Minor: Noticeable issue, easily corrected internally. Moderate: Measurable impact requiring management attention. High: Significant financial loss, severe compliance failure, or operational disruption. Extreme: Critical failure leading to severe financial loss, legal/criminal liability, or severe reputational damage. 3. The Audit Risk Model To determine how deep an audit investigation needs to be, auditors rely on the Audit Risk Model. Audit risk is the probability that an auditor might express a clean opinion when material misstatements or irregularities actually exist.
$$\text{Audit Risk} = \text{Inherent Risk (IR)} \times \text{Control Risk (CR)} \times \text{Detection Risk (DR)}$$
+-------------------------------------------------------+| AUDIT RISK || Risk of giving an improper/incorrect opinion |+-------------------------------------------------------+|+---------------------------------+---------------------------------+| |[ Entity Risk Profile ] [ Auditor Control ]| |+-------+-------+ +-------+-------+| | | |+----+----+ +----+----+ +----+----+| Inherent| | Control | | Detection|| Risk | | Risk | | Risk |+---------+ +---------+ +---------+Natural risk Failure of Auditor'swithout controls internal system sampling error Breaking Down the Components Inherent Risk (IR): The susceptibility of an account balance or transaction type to a material misstatement, assuming there are no related internal controls (e.g., complex pay fixations, non-routine manual payments, or cash-handling units). Control Risk (CR): The risk that a material misstatement will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely basis by the entity’s internal control system (e.g., approving bills without supervisory review or failing to reconcile bank accounts). Detection Risk (DR): The risk that the auditor’s own procedures (sampling size, substantive testing, analytical review) fail to detect a material misstatement that exists. Crucial Rule: The auditor cannot change Inherent Risk or Control Risk—these belong to the audited entity. However, if IR and CR are assessed as high, the auditor must reduce Detection Risk by increasing sample sizes, performing tests at year-end rather than interim, and deploying experienced specialists.
4. The RBIA Execution Process & Planning Roadmap A successful risk-based audit follows a structured, six-stage lifecycle:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+| 1. Strategic Review || Understand government priorities, statutory mandate, and performance periods. |+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+|v+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+| 2. Entity & Control Review || Evaluate organizational structure, internal manuals, and process controls. |+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+|v+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+| 3. Annual Audit Plan Preparation || Map overall objectives, resource allocation, and team deployments. |+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+|v+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+| 4. Unit Risk Assessment & Categorization || Segment into Business Units; score risks from 1 (Low) to 5 (Extreme). |+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+|v+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+| 5. Detailed Audit Program Execution || Perform field testing, review assertions, and verify compliance controls. |+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+|v+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+| 6. Audit Reporting & Feedback Loop || Issue findings, recommend corrective actions, and update risk registers. |+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ 5. Common Financial & Compliance Errors Found in Government Internal Audits During field audits, recurring errors across payroll, procurement, statutory deductions, and asset management consistently inflate Control Risk. Below is a detailed breakdown of 21 common audit findings identified across public sector units.
A. Payroll, Allowances & Retirement Compliance Pay Arrear Calculation Errors: Inaccurate computation of back-pay or arrear bills caused by misunderstanding rules or manual entry errors. Incorrect CGEGIS/CGHS Deductions: Under-deduction or non-deduction of monthly contributions toward the Central Government Employees Group Insurance Scheme or Central Government Health Scheme. Improper Retirement Checks & Bhavishya Non-Compliance: Omitting pre-retirement verification of service books, leading to overpayments. Pension papers must be submitted via the Bhavishya portal at least 6 months prior to retirement. Non-Recovery of Penal Interest: Failing to charge and recover penal interest from employees who hold unspent advance funds beyond the permitted time frame. B. Procurement & Travel Lapses Procurement Outside GeM: Purchasing goods or services outside the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) without generating a valid Non-Availability Certificate (NAC). Non-Compliance in Outsourced Services: Disregarding established guidelines for hiring contract workers, engaging private vehicles, or obtaining required performance security. Unauthorized Air Ticket Purchases: Booking air travel through unapproved travel portals or third-party agents rather than authorized government channels. Class of Travel Violations: Employees traveling in a higher class (e.g., Business Class) than allowed by their pay level entitlement. Non-Revalidation of Performance Bank Guarantees (PBG): Failing to monitor and extend the validity of PBGs before they expire during an active contract. Non-Disposal of Unserviceable Assets: Retaining worn-out or unserviceable vehicles and machinery on balance sheets rather than initiating timely condemnation and auction procedures. Staff Car Record Discrepancies: Improper logbook maintenance, unverified fuel consumption receipts, or private usage of official vehicles. C. Statutory Deductions, Records & Financial Controls TDS on GST Non-Deduction: Failing to deduct Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on GST for vendor payments crossing statutory thresholds. Income Tax TDS Errors: Incorrect computation or late deposit of Income Tax TDS on contract payments or salaries. Missing Utilization Certificates (UCs): Failure to obtain or submit UCs for grants and funds allocated for specific scheme implementation. Missing Bank Final Certificates: Inability to secure final bank verification certificates required to validate interest earnings or tax rebates. General Arithmetical Miscalculations: Subtotal errors, wrong multiplication rates on bills, or ledger posting errors. 6. Actionable Audit Checklist To streamline field reviews and minimize control risks, internal audit teams should check these specific items against every audited unit:
Audit Focus Area Mandatory Verification Document / System Check Procurement GeM Non-Availability Certificate (if bought off-portal) Contract Security Expiry tracking ledger for Performance Bank Guarantees (PBGs) Travel Claims Air tickets issued exclusively by authorized agencies Tax Compliance Monthly TDS returns and deduction receipts for Income Tax & GST Grants & Allocations Signed Utilization Certificates (UCs) for spent funds Retirement Process Submission confirmation on the Bhavishya Portal (6-month rule) Vehicle Management Vehicle logbook approvals and condemnation files for idle assets Summary Shifting to a Risk-Based Internal Audit model transforms internal audit from a passive oversight function into an active driver of governance and internal control. By understanding the Audit Risk Model, evaluating Inherent Risk, and targeting high-risk operational areas, audit teams can protect public resources, ensure statutory compliance, and eliminate systemic errors before they escalate.

Introduction When state austerity directives, strict budget restrictions during a Vote on Account period, and rigid biometric attendance mandates collide, essential public administration processes can ground to a complete halt.
This case study demonstrates the iterative drafting of an official office noting for the Directorate of Local Fund Audit (DLFA)[cite: 1]. The objective is to present a crisp, highly structured executive note seeking administrative waivers, emergency fund releases, or explicit deferment directives from higher authorities to safeguard central grants under the 16th Finance Commission (XVI FC)[cite: 1].
Phase 1: Drafting the Structural Baseline Using standard departmental noting frameworks, the core dilemma is divided into structured executive sections covering regulatory mandates, financial risks, operational friction, and quantitative trade-offs[cite: 1].
Official Note Draft File Tracking Reference Number: DLFA/AUD-TOUR/2026/089
Originating Department: Directorate of Local Fund Audit (DLFA), Internal Audit / Local Fund Audit Section
Subject: Seeking Critical Exemptions, Budgetary Release, and Operational Directives for the Commencement of Annual Audit Tours to Safeguard XVI Finance Commission Grants
This file has been initiated following the recent executive briefing with the Secretary regarding the operational deadlock currently halting the Annual Audit Plan. Immediate administrative directives are required to resolve the conflict between mandatory statutory audit obligations and prevailing state austerity mandates, strict Vote on Account restrictions, and biometric attendance regulations, which collectively threaten a total paralysis of field operations.
The Local Fund Audit (LFA) Act and accompanying service rules mandate a non-negotiable schedule for the physical audit of all Gram Panchayats, Zilla Panchayats, and Urban Local Bodies. Under Section 19 of the Act, consolidated audit reports must be submitted to the State Legislative Assembly within strict statutory timelines. Furthermore, central guidelines dictate that all finalized audits must be directly uploaded and certified on the central AuditOnline portal. Physical verification of accounts and assets is a legal prerequisite; skipping or delaying field verification invalidates the certification process.
Compliance with the local fund audit timeline is a mandatory prerequisite for the drawdown of federal resources under the 16th Finance Commission (XVI FC) guidelines. Failure to conduct these audits will result in an immediate lapse of central funds, directly jeopardizing the state’s projected receipt of 30% of the Basic Grant of the XVI FC and the Performance Grant of the 6th SFC for the current fiscal year. Inaction will freeze local development blocks and severely strain the state’s overall revenue position.
The deployment of the five active audit teams is currently impeded by conflicting administrative mandates. State austerity directives enforcing inter-district travel restrictions prevent the sequential continuity of block-level auditing. Additionally, the mandatory weekend ban on government vehicles eliminates 54 days (27 Saturdays and 27 Sundays) from the standard 190-day touring calendar. Quantitative analysis establishes that this restriction causes an immediate 30% reduction in operational capacity, leaving a critical portion of the statutory mandate unfulfilled. The resultant backlog will delay legislative submissions beyond the legal deadline. Logistical compounding factors further aggravate the crisis: AEBAS biometric attendance rules require daily verification at the head office, rendering multi-day field tours technically impossible under current software parameters.
To circumvent the weekend vehicle ban and maintain the audit schedule, the sole alternative is the outsourcing of logistics through the commercial hire of private taxis for all five field teams. A formal cost-benefit analysis indicates that hiring commercial transit across a prolonged 190-day cycle will vastly escalate the department’s operational expenses compared to utilizing the existing government fleet. However, during the current Vote on Account period, the department faces absolute budgetary shortfalls. No resources have been released against the regular budget allocation for Petrol, Oil, and Lubricants (POL), High-Speed Diesel (HSD), or Travelling Allowance/Daily Allowance (TA/DA) components. The department possesses zero financial headroom to absorb either regular operational costs or escalated commercial hire charges without a dedicated emergency allocation.
In view of the detailed Audit Tour Programme (PUC4) and the corresponding statutory requirements, specific administrative orders are requested on the following mutually exclusive options:
Option A (Administrative Exemption): Grant a special travel waiver designating DLFA audit tours as an “Essential Fiscal Service,” thereby authorizing the five audit teams to utilize government vehicles on weekends and across districts, alongside a temporary AEBAS biometric exemption to regularize field attendance. Option B (Provisional Resource Allocation): Approve the commercial hire of private taxis for the audit teams to bypass vehicle restrictions, backed by an immediate, provisional release of emergency funds to cover the escalated hire charges, POL/HSD, and TA/DA components despite current Vote on Account constraints. Option C (Formal Deferment of Operations): Order the formal deferment of all field audit tours until the full budget is passed and austerity measures are relaxed, with the explicit understanding that the administration accepts the resultant statutory violations under the LFA Act and the direct financial liability of the lapsed XVI FC and 6th SFC grants. Submitted for perusal and specific orders.
Accounts Officer, IA/LFA
Phase 2: Incorporating Quantitative Logistics Analysis To provide higher decision-making authorities with precise financial clarity, concrete calculations comparing outsourced commercial transport versus standard government fleet deployment were integrated directly into the note.
Comparative Financial Analysis Commercial Taxi Alternative:
$$\text{Rate} = \text{Rs } 3,000 / \text{day}$$
$$\text{Operational Base} = 200 \text{ days} \times 5 \text{ teams}$$
$$\text{Total Expenditure} = 3,000 \times 200 \times 5 = \mathbf{\text{Rs } 30,000,000 \text{ (Rs 30.00 Lakhs)}}$$
Government Fleet (POL/HSD) Alternative:
$$\text{Rate} = \text{Rs } 94 / \text{km}$$
$$\text{Operational Base} = 150 \text{ km/month} \times 8 \text{ months} \times 5 \text{ teams}$$
$$\text{Total Expenditure} = 94 \times 150 \times 8 \times 5 = \mathbf{\text{Rs } 564,000 \text{ (Rs 5.64 Lakhs)}}$$
Integrated Comparative Table Transport Logistics Option Unit Cost Parameters Operational Base Total Projected Expenditure Outsourced Commercial Taxis Rs 3,000 per day per team 200 Days × 5 Teams Rs 3,000,000 Government Fleet (POL/HSD) Rs 94 per km (at 150 km per month) 8 Months × 5 Teams Rs 564,000 Net Budgetary Deficit / Variance Rs 2,436,000 Financial Variance: Opting for commercial hire introduces an escalated expense burden of Rs 24,36,000 over standard departmental fleet operations.
Key Takeaways for Official Secretariat Drafting Precision Over Rhetoric: Public administration notes require concise, objective summaries stating operational facts, legislative mandates, and precise financial impacts without unnecessary conversational filler. Actionable Decision Matrices: Offering mutually exclusive administrative choices (Exemption, Emergency Funding, or Formal Deferment) obligates higher executive offices to issue explicit, legally binding directives. Data-Driven Financial Comparisons: Structuring cost projections into explicit markdown tables enables instant clarity during administrative review.

The Government of Sikkim’s Finance Department officially issued Notification No. 03/FIN/ADM through Extraordinary Gazette No. 303. Enacted under clause (3) of Article 166 of the Constitution of India, the Sikkim Government Vehicle Procurement and Maintenance Rules, 2025 establish clear procedures, financial ceilings, entitlements, and operational guidelines governing all official state vehicles.
1. Key Definitions & Operational Framework The rules apply to all government vehicles—including two-wheelers, passenger cars, utility pick-ups, and heavy vehicles—across state departments.
Cumulative Expenditure: Represents the progressive total expenditure incurred on repair and maintenance over the life of the vehicle.
Financial Year: Defined as a 12-month period starting from the original purchase date of the vehicle.
Head of Department (HOD): A government servant in the rank of Secretary or above who heads the department.
Drawing and Disbursing Officer (DDO): An officer designated by the Finance Department to draw bills and handle state payments.
2. Vehicle Entitlements by Officer Level Rule 10 outlines strict rules for purchasing and allocating vehicles based on official designated ranks:
Level of Officers Vehicle Entitlement Group A Level 22 and above / Corresponding All India Service (AIS) Officers Scorpio N ZS MT or any other SUV approved by the Govt. Group A Level 20–21 / Corresponding AIS Officers Scorpio Classic S11 or any other SUV approved by the Govt. Group A Level 19 / Corresponding AIS Officers Bolero NEO/N10 or any other vehicle approved by the Govt. Gazetted Touring Officers below Group A Level 19 Bolero B6 (2WD) or approved vehicle (requires prior approval of the Chief Secretary) New or replacement vehicles can only be procured with the prior concurrence of the Finance Department (and Home Department where required), along with sanction from the Chief Minister via the Chief Secretary.
3. Financial Limits & Sanctioning Authorities Minor & Private Garage Repairs Head of Departments (HOD) and Head of Offices (HOO) can authorize repair work in private garages approved by the Sikkim Nationalised Transport (SNT) Division without prior technical bill verification, provided cost limits are respected:
Two Wheelers: Maximum ₹5,000 per instance; capped at ₹10,000 per annum. All Other Vehicles: Maximum ₹15,000 per instance; capped at ₹50,000 per annum. Special Accessories & VVIP/VIP Vehicles Safety Accessories: HODs may sanction up to ₹10,000 once during a vehicle’s lifetime for functional accessories like rain guards or mudguards. Decorative items (alloy wheels, custom searchlights, media players) are prohibited. VVIP / VIP Vehicles: Special fittings adhere strictly to SNT technical specifications. HODs have full powers to sanction up to ₹50,000 over the lifetime of the vehicle. 4. Routine Servicing, Accessories & Tyre Replacements Routine maintenance items (servicing, tyres, seat covers, and mats) do not count toward the cumulative repair ceiling but must be entered into the vehicle’s official history sheet.
Servicing Cost Restrictions Servicing costs (including lubricants) are restricted per session:
Two Wheelers: ₹2,000 Gypsy / Car / Van / Others: ₹10,000 Bolero / Utility / Pickup: ₹15,000 Scorpio / SUVs / Heavy Vehicles: ₹20,000 Innova / Fortuner: ₹25,000 Servicing frequency is capped at once every 3 months / 8,000 km for touring vehicles, or once every 6 months / 8,000 km for local duty vehicles.
Tyre & Tube Replacement Thresholds Up to four tyres/tubes can be replaced once the following mileage thresholds are reached:
Utility / Pickup: 17,000 km Light Motor Vehicles / SUVs / Two Wheelers: 20,000 km Heavy Vehicles: 15,000 km Interior Furnishing Costs Mats: Maximum ₹6,000 for SUVs (3 pcs) or ₹4,500 for others (replacement permitted only after 2 years). Seat Covers: Complete seat covers (including stitching) are capped at ₹10,000 (replacement allowed only after 3 years). 5. Monthly Vehicle User Charges Officers or functionaries using government vehicles for both official and private purposes pay a monthly deduction directly from their salaries:
Purchase Cost of Vehicle Monthly User Charge Up to ₹10,00,000/- ₹1,000/- ₹10,00,001/- to ₹15,00,000/- ₹1,500/- Above ₹15,00,000/- ₹2,000/- Shared Usage: Shared vehicles split the user charge across all assigned officers. Programme Vehicles: Officers using programme vehicles pay 50% of the standard rate. Exemptions: Vehicles assigned to the Governor, Chief Minister, Chief Justice, High Court Judges, along with ambulances, hearses, buses, trucks, fire tenders, and police pilot/escort vehicles are exempt. 6. Repairs Following Accidents & Work Guarantees Accident Repairs: If repair costs exceed ₹60,000 following an accident, the proposal requires SNT technical examination alongside Home and Finance Department concurrences. An FIR, police cause report, and departmental inquiry report must accompany the claim. Approved accident costs do not count toward the annual vehicle repair limit. Personal/Unauthorized Use: Accident repair costs resulting from personal use or unauthorized drivers will not be borne by the government. Repair Guarantees: Garages must provide a mandatory 1-year guarantee for major engine repairs, minor engine repairs, and gearbox repairs. 7. Vehicle Condemnation & Public Auction Procedures A vehicle can be condemned only after receiving a technical fitness certificate from the SNT Division stating that it is no longer fit for economical use.
Lifespan Criteria for Condemnation Standard Motor Vehicles (<18 HP): 1.50 lakh km run or 10 years of service (whichever is completed later). Fire Service Vehicles: 5,000 hours of static operation or 10 years in service (24 km run is treated as equivalent to 1 hour stationary operation). Disposal Process Condemned vehicles are disposed of through public auctions managed by the Transport Department. Mandatory public auction notices must be published across print and digital media with at least one month’s advance notice. All auction proceeds are credited directly back into the official Government Revenue Head.
8. Schedule I: Progressive Annual Repair Ceilings Rule 3 mandates that total progressive repair expenditures over a 10-year lifespan must not exceed the cumulative limits listed below (represented in Lakhs of Rupees):

Sikkim Panchayat Financial Rules: A Comprehensive Overview Local governance in Sikkim operates under a well-structured framework to manage funds, maintain accounts, and ensure financial accountability across local self-governments. This detailed post outlines the full text of both the Sikkim Gram Panchayat (Financial) Rules, 2003 and the Sikkim Zilla Panchayat (Financial) Rules, 2001, including their respective official notifications, schedules, and amendment notifications.
Part 1: Sikkim Gram Panchayat (Financial) Rules, 2003 RURAL DEVELOPMENT DEPARTMENT
GOVERNMENT OF SIKKIM
GANGTOK, SIKKIM.
No.35(159)93-94/RDD/P-III/33.
Dated: 10.07.2003.
NOTIFICATION In exercise of the powers conferred by Section 130 of the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993 (Act No.6 of 1993), the State Government hereby makes the following rules, namely: -
1. Short title and commencement. (1) These rules may be called the Sikkim Gram Panchayat (Financial) Rules, 2003.
(2) They shall come into force at once.
2. Definition. (1) In these rules, unless the context otherwise requires:-
(a) “Act” means the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993.
(b) “Secretary” means the Secretary to the Govt. of Sikkim in the Rural Development Department or any other Officer designated as such by the State Government.
(c) “Schedule” means the schedule appended to these rules.
(2) Words defined in the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993 but not defined in these rules shall have the same meaning as respectively assigned to them in the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993.
3. Establishment of Gram Panchayat Fund. (1) The Gram Panchayat Fund established under sub-section (1) of section 39 of the Act shall be held in the Saving Bank Account with the State Bank of Sikkim or any other Nationalized Bank having its branch at the respective District Headquarter and also at Gangtok.
(2) All monies received by the Gram Panchayat from various sources as indicated at clause (a) to (g) of sub-section (1) of section 39 of the Act shall be deposited by the Sachiva in the Gram Panchayat Fund Account on the same day and entry made in the Cash Book as required under rule 4 of these rules.
Provided that where it is not possible to deposit the cash or cheque in the Gram Panchayat Fund account, the Sachiva shall keep the same under his safe custody and deposit the sums on the next working dayin the Bank where such account is maintained.
Provided further that no sums in cash or cheque shall be kept without depositing the same in the account for more than three days without obtaining the approval of the Secretary, Rural Development Department.
(3) The Account shall be maintained in the name and style of “Gram Panchayat Fund” duly prefixing the name of the Gram Panchayat and subject to the general control of the Sachiva and jointly operated by the Sabhapati and the Sachiva.
(4) The Gram Panchayat may after passing a resolution and after taking into account the liquidity position invests part or whole of the Gram Panchayat Fund in Government approved securities and investments. Provided that the approval of the Secretary, Rural Development Department shall be obtained before such investment is made.
4. Maintenance of Cash Book. (1) It shall be the responsibity of the Sachiva to ensure maintenance of Cash Book in the Form as specified in Schedule-A and its safe custody.
(2) All transactions shall be entered in the Cash Book as soon as they occur and in order of their occurrence. The pages of each book shall be numbered and the number of pages shall be certified by the Sachiva.
(3) All receipts and payments shall be duly supported by vouchers which shall be numbered and their number shall be recorded in the Cash Book. All receipts and payments vouchers shall be kept separately in order of its number.
(4) The Cash Book shall be closed monthly.
(5) Erasure or over-writing of any entry in the Cash Book shall not be allowed. All incorrect entries shall be cancelled by drawing the pen across the incorrect entry and inserting the correct entry with the initials of the concerned official.
5. Reconciliation of balance. (1) The Sachiva shall prepare the Bank Reconciliation Statement in the form given in Schedule D on a monthly basis.
(2) In the event of non-reconciliation of the balance, the Sachiva shall bring this fact to the notice of the Sabhapati and the Secretary, Rural Development Department.
6. Procedure for drawal of money from the account. (1) No money shall be drawn from the Bank unless it is required for immediate disbursement.
(2) All expenses and payment for which the fund is proposed to be withdrawn should be duly approved and sanctioned by the Secretary, Rural Development Department or by any Officer to whom such power has been delegated.
(3) All drawals shall be made through cheque only and after making the necessary entries in the Cash Book and recording the details of payment on the counterfoil of the cheque.
(4) A sum not exceeding Rs.500.00 (Rupees Five Hundred) only shall be kept as Imprest Fund with the Sachiva of the Gram Panchayat duly authorized by the Sabhapati. The total expenditure out of the Imprest Fund shall be accounted for on the last working day of the month and sum equal of the expenditure shall be transferred to the Imprest Fund so as to make the closing balance equal to the opening balance of the month. However, the total expenditure on such petty accounts shall not exceed Rs.2000.00 annually. An Imprest register shall be maintained for such Imprest Fund.
(5) For grants/funds released by the State/Central Government, Utilisation Certificate should invariably be submitted to the Department/agency releasing the grant with a copy to the Secretary, Rural Development Department. Failure shall result in withholding of further grants/funds.
7. Preparation and maintenance of accounts. (1) The accounts of the Gram Panchayat shall be maintained in the manner specified in these rules and in the forms set out in the Schedules appended herewith.
(2) It shall be mandatory for each Gram Panchayat to prepare and maintain the following books of accounts and statements in the prescribed forms as specified in the schedules appended to these rules:-
(a) Cash Book.
(b) Monthly Receipt & Payment Register.
(c) Annual Receipt & Payment Account.
(d) Monthly Reconciliation Statement.
(e) Inventory Register for Moveable Assets.
(f) Inventory Register for Immoveable Assets.
(g) Balance Sheet.
8. Preparation of annual budget & estimates of receipts & payments. (1) Every Gram Panchayat shall prepare a budget of its estimated receipts and expenditure for the next financial year during the month of August each year in the form specified and appended to these rules and submit it to the Secretary, Rural Development Department, for its approval.
Provided that a copy of the estimate shall be submitted to the District Planning Committee, if the Committee has been constituted for the district.
(2) The State Government shall approve the budget of the Gram Panchayat, with or without modification and such approval shall be communicated to the Gram Panchayat and the District Planning Committee, if constituted, before the commencement of the next financial year.
(3) No expenditure shall be incurred unless the budget is approved by the State Government.
(4) No re-appropriation shall be allowed without the approval of the State Government.
9. Authorities competent to sanction & incur expenditure & extent of their powers. (1) The power to incur expenditure out of the provision made in the proved budget and the extent of such power shall be in accordance with the delegation of financial powers specified in Schedule L [VERIFY: Referred to as Schedule F in tables].
(2) The Gram Panchayat shall discuss and approve any expenditure during its meetings held in accordance with Section 20 and transact its business in accordance with Section 22 of the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993. Sanction of an expenditure, if required, shall be by a resolution passed by the majority of the members.
(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in these rules, the State Government may confer on any authority specific power to incur expenditure on specific items and upon such conferment, the said authority shall exercise such power for specific purpose only.
10. Custody, preservation of books & records & procedures for destruction. (1) The Sachiva shall ensure the safe custody of all books of accounts and records of the Gram Panchayat and shall produce them for inspection the auditors and any other officer/agency authorized by the Secretary.
(2) No books of accounts, vouchers or record shall be destroyed without the approval of the Secretary, Rural Development Department.
11. Audit of Accounts. The Sabhapati shall produce or cause to be produced, to the auditor, all such accounts and related records of the funds of the Gram Panchayat concerned as may be required on behalf of the State Government and/or the Auditor General of India under section 20(1) of the Auditor General of India (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971.
The Audit Report shall be placed before the Zilla Panchayat and the Gram Panchayat within 30 days, if necessary, by calling a special meeting.
12. Removal of doubt. When doubt arises as to the interpretation of any provision of these rules, the matter shall be referred to the Secretary, Rural Development Department.
R. Ongmu,
Secretary to the Government of Sikkim,
Rural Development Department.

Sikkim Gram Panchayat (Financial) Amendment Rules, 2004 RURAL MANAGEMENT & DEVELOPMENT DEPARTMENT
GOVERNMENT OF SIKKIM
GANGTOK, SIKKIM
No.746/RM&DD.
Dated: 08.02.2005.
NOTIFICATION In exercise of the powers conferred by section 130 of the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993 (6 of 1993), the State Government is pleased to make the following rules further to amend the Sikkim Gram Panchayat (Financial) Rules, 2004, namely :-
1. Short title and commencement. (1) These rules may be called the Sikkim Gram Panchayat (Financial) Amendment Rules, 2004.
(2) They shall come into force at once.
2. Amendment of rule 6. In the Sikkim Panchayat (Financial) Rules, 2004 (hereinafter referred to as the said rules), for sub-rule (2) of rule 6, the following shall be substituted, namely :-
“All expenses and payments from the Gram Panchayat Fund shall be in accordance with the approved budget of the Gram Panchayat and the delegation of powers under schedule- I, appended to these rules.”
3. Amendment of rule 7. In the said rules, in rule 7, after sub-rule (2), the following shall be inserted, namely :-
“(3) The Rural Development Assistant or any such Officer as may be appointed by the State Government for the purpose, shall assist the Sachiva in preparation and maintenance of accounts in the prescribed forms. All books of accounts, statements, vouchers, registers, etc, relating to the operation of the Gram Panchayat Fund shall be kept in the custody of the Rural Development Assistant in the Gram Panchayat Office.”
V.B. Pathak, IAS,
Secretary to the Government of Sikkim,
Rural Management & Development Department.
Part 2: Sikkim Zilla Panchayat (Financial) Rules, 2001 GOVERNMENT OF SIKKIM
RURAL DEVELOPMENT DEPARTMENT
No.35(35)97-98/6/RDD/P.
Dated: 24.8.2001.
NOTIFICATION In exercise of the powers conferred by section 130 of the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993 (6 of 1993), the State Government hereby makes the following rules, namely:-
1. Short title and commencement. (1) These rules may be called the Sikkim Zilla Panchayat (Financial) Rules, 2001.
(2) They shall come into force at once.
2. Definitions (1) In these rules, unless the context otherwise requires:-
(a) “Act” means the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993.
(b) “Secretary” means the Secretary to the Government in the Rural Development Department or any other officer designated as such by the State Government.
(c) “Schedule” means the Schedules appended to these rules.
(2) Words defined in the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993 but not defined in these rules shall have the same meanings as respectively assigned to them in the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993.
3. Establishment of Zilla Panchayat Fund. (1) The Zilla Panchayat fund established under sub-section (1) of section 76 of the Act shall be held in the Savings Bank Account with the State Bank of Sikkim or any other Nationalised Bank having its branch at the respective District Headquarter and also at Gangtok.
(2) All monies received by the Zilla Panchayat from various sources as indicated at clause (a) to (g) of sub-section (1) of section 76 of the Act shall be deposited by the Sachiva in the Zilla Panchayat Fund Account on the same day and the entry made in the Cash Book as required under rule 4 of these rules.
Provided that where it is not possible to deposit the cash or cheque in the Zilla Panchayat Fund Account, the Sachiva will keep the same under his safe custody and deposit the sums on the next working day in the bank where such account is maintained.
Provided further that no sums in cash or cheque, shall be kept without depositing the same in the account for more than three months without obtaining the approval of the Secretary, Rural Development Department.
(3) The Account shall be maintained in the name and style of “District Zilla Panchayat Fund” duly prefixing the name of Zilla Panchayat and subject to general control of Zilla Panchayat, shall be operated jointly by the Adhakshya and the Sachiva.
Provided that where a particular payment or drawal has been authorized and approved by the Secretary, Rural Development Department to do so as per the delegation of powers under these rules, Sachiva is authorized to sign cheques for payment for an amount not exceeding Rs. 50,000/-
(4) The Zilla Panchayat may after passing a resolution in this behalf and after taking in to account the liquidity position, invest part of whole or Zilla Panchayat fund in the Government approved securities and investment.
4. Maintenance of Cash Book. (1) It shall be the responsibility of the Sachiva to ensure maintenance of the Cash Book as specified in Schedule-A and in his safe custody.
(2) All transactions shall be entered in Cash Book as soon as they occur in order of their occurrence. The page of each book shall be numbered. They total number of pages in the book shall be certified by the Sachiva.
(3) All receipts and payments shall be duly supported by vouchers which shall be numbered and their number, shall be recorded in the Cash Book. All receipt and payment vouchers shall be kept separately in the order of their number and date.
(4) The cash book shall be closed on the last date of each calendar year or earlier and the balance shall be brought forward and shown as the opening on the first day of the next month.
(5) An erasure or over writing of an entry in the cash book shall not be allowed. All incorrect entries shall be cancelled by drawing the pen once across the incorrect entry and inserting the correct one under the initials of concerned official.
5. Reconciliation of balance. (1) After the closure of Cash Book for a particular month, the Sachiva shall cause to be prepared, before the 15th of the following month, a statement of the receipt and expenditure during the month and the closing balance and a copy submitted in the form specified in Schedule-B.
(2) In the event of non-reconciliation of the balance, Sachiva shall make all effort to find cause thereof and shall immediately bring this fact to the notice of Adhakshya and the Secretary.
6. Procedure for drawal of money from the Account. (1) No money shall be drawn from the Bank unless it is required for immediate disbursement.
(2) All the expenses and payment for which the fund is proposed to be withdrawn should be duly approved and sanctioned by the Secretary, Rural Development Department under the provision of these rules or under the specific authorization of the Government.
(3) All the drawals shall be made through cheque only after making the necessary entries in the cash book and recording details of payment on the counterfoil in the cheque.
(4) A sum not exceeding Rs.2000.00 (Rupees two thousand) only be kept as imprest fund with the official of the Zilla Panchayat duly authorized by the Sachiva. The total expenditure from the imprest fund shall be accounted for on the last working day of the month and sum equal of the total expenditure shall be transferred to imprest fund so as to make the closing balance equal to the opening balance of the month. However, the total expenditure on such petty accounts shall not exceed Rs. 5000/- annually out of imprest fund. A separate record shall be maintained for drawal of such imprest fund.
(5) For grants/funds released by the State/Central Government, Utilization Certificate should invariable be submitted on quarterly basis to the Secretary, Rural Development Department. Failure to do so shall result in withholding of further grants/funds.
7. Preparation and maintenance of accounts. (1) The accounts of the Zilla Panchayat Funds shall be maintained in the manner specified in the rule and the various forms set out in the schedules.
(2) It shall be mandatory for each Zilla Panchayat to prepare and maintain the following Books of Accounts and the Statement in the prescribed forms as specified in the schedules appended to these rules;-
(a) Cash Book.
(b) Ledger for recording item wise income and expenditure with the details of sub-head, minor and major head.
(c) Income and expenditure account and balance sheet.
(d) Inventory Register for fixed and non consumable assets and office equipments.
(e) Cheque drawn register.
(3) In addition to major and minor heads, prescribed for preparation of Income and Expenditure Accounts and Annual Budget estimates of income and expenditure, the Zilla Panchayat may open suitable sub-heads under the minor heads concerned to exhibit the expenditure on different activities and income from different sources. No major and minor heads should, however, be added or removed without permission of the Secretary, Rural Development Department.
(4) The Zilla Panchayat shall prepare at the end of each financial year a receipt and payment account, income and expenditure account and balance sheets to prepare a true and fair picture of the affairs of Zilla Panchayat and present the same to Zilla Panchayat in its meeting within three months from the closure of financial year and a copy of the same shall be submitted to Secretary.
Provided that the Secretary may allow a relaxation of two months for submission of actual accounts as above if he is satisfied that the delay has taken place due to unavoidable circumstances.
8. Preparation of Annual Budget and Estimates of Receipts & Payments. (1) Every Zilla Panchayat shall prepare in each year a budget of its estimated receipts and expenditure for the next financial year before the last day of August in the form receipts and specified in Schedule E and submit it to the Secretary for approval of the State Government.
Provided that before submission to the State Government final approval the budget shall first be placed before the Zilla Panchayat in its meeting for consideration and approval.
(2) The State Government shall approve the Budget of the Zilla Panchayat, with or without modification and such approval shall be communicated to Zilla Panchayat before the commencement of the next financial year.
(3) No expenditure shall be incurred unless the Budget is approved by the State Government.
(4) The Zilla Panchayat shall forward its proposal to the State Government for re-appropriation under one budget head and the State Government, after consideration of the proposal, may allow such re-appropriation subject to the conditions it may deem necessary to impose.
9. Authorities competent to sanction & incur expenditure & extent of their powers. (1) The power to incur expenditure out of the provision made in the approved budget and to the extent of such power shall be in accordance with the delegation of financial powers specified in Schedule - F.
(2) The Zilla Panchayat shall in its meeting select 3 (three) members in addition to Adhakshaya and Up-Adhakshaya to form an Executive Committee which shall meet as often and desirable to discuss all matters other than routine administrative matters and also accord sanction wherever sanction is required to be accorded by the Executive Committee in accordance with the scheme of delegation of power specified in Schedule - F.
The Executive Committee shall be responsible for supervision of all works and scheme of Zilla Panchayat.
(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in this rule, the State Government may confer on any authority specific power to incur expenditure on specific items and upon such conferment, the said authority shall exercise such power for specified purpose only.
10. Custody, preservation of books and record & procedure for destruction. (1) The Sachiva shall ensure the safe custody of all the books of accounts and records of Zilla Panchayat and shall produce them for inspection to the auditors and any other officer/agency authorized by the Secretary. The following shall be the permanent record of Zilla Panchayat and shall be kept in record perpetually:
(a) Cash Book.
(b) Bank Pass Book.
(c) Annual Accounts, viz., receipts and payments account of Income and Expenditure Statement and Balance Sheet.
(d) Audit Report.
(e) Assets Register.
(2) Any other record not listed in sub-rule (1) above shall be preserved for the next 5 (five) years and thereafter, can be destroyed after their audit of accounts of that particular period that taken place as per the guidelines specified by the State Government in that behalf from time to time.
11. Audit of accounts. It shall be the duty of Adhakshya and Sachiva to get its accounts audited, whenever called upon to do so by the auditors appointment in its behalf by the State Government and extend all assistance to the auditors to facilitate examination of audit of accounts.
12. Removal of doubt. When a doubt arises as to the interpretation of any provision of these rules, the matter shall be referred to the Secretary, Rural Development Department whose decision thereon, shall be final and binding.
R. Ongmu,
Secretary to the Government of Sikkim,
Rural Development Department.

Government of Sikkim Rural Development Department Notification No.35(35)97-98/6/RDD/P.
Dated 24.8.2001.
NOTIFICATION In exercise of the powers conferred by section 130 of the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993 (6 of 1993), the State Government hereby makes the following rules, namely:-
1. Short title and commencement. (1) These rules may be called the Sikkim Zilla Panchayat (Financial) Rules, 2001.
(2) They shall come into force at once.
2. Definitions (1) In these rules, unless the context otherwise requires:-
(a) “Act” means the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993.
(b) “Secretary” means the Secretary to the Government in the Rural Development Department or any other officer designated as such by the State Government.
(c) “Schedule” means the Schedules appended to these rules.
(2) Words defined in the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993 but not defined in these rules shall have the same meanings as respectively assigned to them in the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1993.
3. Establishment of Zilla Panchayat Fund. (1) The Zilla Panchayat fund established under sub-section (1) of section 76 of the Act shall be held in the Savings Bank Account with the State Bank of Sikkim or any other Nationalised Bank having its branch at the respective District Headquarter and also at Gangtok.
(2) All monies received by the Zilla Panchayat from various sources as indicated at clause (a) to (g) of sub-section (1) of section 76 of the Act shall be deposited by the Sachiva in the Zilla Panchayat Fund Account on the same day and the entry made in the Cash Book as required under rule 4 of these rules.
Provided that where it is not possible to deposit the cash or cheque in the Zilla Panchayat Fund Account, the Sachiva will keep the same under his safe custody and deposit the sums on the next working day in the bank where such account is maintained.
Provided further that no sums in cash or cheque, shall be kept without depositing the same in the account for more than three months without obtaining the approval of the Secretary, Rural Development Department.
(3) The Account shall be maintained in the name and style of “District Zilla Panchayat Fund” duly prefixing the name of Zilla Panchayat and subject to general control of Zilla Panchayat, shall be operated jointly by the Adhakshya and the Sachiva.
Provided that where a particular payment or drawal has been authorized and approved by the Secretary, Rural Development Department to do so as per the delegation of powers under these rules, Sachiva is authorized to sign cheques for payment for an amount not exceeding Rs. 50,000/-
(4) The Zilla Panchayat may after passing a resolution in this behalf and after taking in to account the liquidity position, invest part of whole or Zilla Panchayat fund in the Government approved securities and investment.
4. Maintenance of Cash Book. (1) It shall be the responsibility of the Sachiva to ensure maintenance of the Cash Book as specified in Schedule-A and in his safe custody.
(2) All transactions shall be entered in Cash Book as soon as they occur in order of their occurrence. The page of each book shall be numbered. They total number of pages in the book shall be certified by the Sachiva.
(3) All receipts and payments shall be duly supported by vouchers which shall be numbered and their number, shall be recorded in the Cash Book. All receipt and payment vouchers shall be kept separately in the order of their number and date.
(4) The cash book shall be closed on the last date of each calendar year or earlier and the balance shall be brought forward and shown as the opening on the first day of the next month.
(5) An erasure or over writing of an entry in the cash book shall not be allowed. All incorrect entries shall be cancelled by drawing the pen once across the incorrect entry and inserting the correct one under the initials of concerned official.
5. Reconciliation of balance. (1) After the closure of Cash Book for a particular month, the Sachiva shall cause to be prepared, before the 15th of the following month, a statement of the receipt and expenditure during the month and the closing balance and a copy submitted in the form specified in Schedule-B.
(2) In the event of non-reconciliation of the balance, Sachiva shall make all effort to find cause thereof and shall immediately bring this fact to the notice of Adhakshya and the Secretary.
6. Procedure for drawal of money from the Account. (1) No money shall be drawn from the Bank unless it is required for immediate disbursement.
(2) All the expenses and payment for which the fund is proposed to be withdrawn should be duly approved and sanctioned by the Secretary, Rural Development Department under the provision of these rules or under the specific authorization of the Government.
(3) All the drawals shall be made through cheque only after making the necessary entries in the cash book and recording details of payment on the counterfoil in the cheque.
(4) A sum not exceeding Rs.2000.00 (Rupees two thousand) only be kept as imprest fund with the official of the Zilla Panchayat duly authorized by the Sachiva. The total expenditure from the imprest fund shall be accounted for on the last working day of the month and sum equal of the total expenditure shall be transferred to imprest fund so as to make the closing balance equal to the opening balance of the month. However, the total expenditure on such petty accounts shall not exceed Rs. 5000/- annually out of imprest fund. A separate record shall be maintained for drawal of such imprest fund.
(5) For grants/funds released by the State/Central Government, Utilization Certificate should invariable be submitted on quarterly basis to the Secretary, Rural Development Department. Failure to do so shall result in withholding of further grants/funds.
7. Preparation and maintenance of accounts. (1) The accounts of the Zilla Panchayat Funds shall be maintained in the manner specified in the rule and the various forms set out in the schedules.
(2) It shall be mandatory for each Zilla Panchayat to prepare and maintain the following Books of Accounts and the Statement in the prescribed forms as specified in the schedules appended to these rules;-
(a) Cash Book. (b) Ledger for recording item wise income and expenditure with the details of sub-head, minor and major head. (c) Income and expenditure account and balance sheet. (d) Inventory Register for fixed and non consumable assets and office equipments. (e) Cheque drawn register. (3) In addition to major and minor heads, prescribed for preparation of Income and Expenditure Accounts and Annual Budget estimates of income and expenditure, the Zilla Panchayat may open suitable sub-heads under the minor heads concerned to exhibit the expenditure on different activities and income from different sources. No major and minor heads should, however, be added or removed without permission of the Secretary, Rural Development Department.
(4) The Zilla Panchayat shall prepare at the end of each financial year a receipt and payment account, income and expenditure account and balance sheets to prepare a true and fair picture of the affairs of Zilla Panchayat and present the same to Zilla Panchayat in its meeting within three months from the closure of financial year and a copy of the same shall be submitted to Secretary.
Provided that the Secretary may allow a relaxation of two months for submission of actual accounts as above if he is satisfied that the delay has taken place due to unavoidable circumstances.
8. Preparation of Annual Budget and Estimates of Receipts & Payments. (1) Every Zilla Panchayat shall prepare in each year a budget of its estimated receipts and expenditure for the next financial year before the last day of August in the form receipts and specified in Schedule E and submit it to the Secretary for approval of the State Government.
Provided that before submission to the State Government final approval the budget shall first be placed before the Zilla Panchayat in its meeting for consideration and approval.
(2) The Sate Government shall approve the Budget of the Zilla Panchayat, with or without modification and such approval shall be communicated to Zilla Panchayat before the commencement of the next financial year.
(3) No expenditure shall be incurred unless the Budget is approved by the State Government.
(4) The Zilla Panchayat shall forward its proposal to the State Government for re-appropriation under one budget head and the State Government, after consideration of the proposal, may allow such re-appropriation subject to the conditions it may deem necessary to impose.
9. Authorities competent to sanction & incur expenditure & extent of their powers. (1) The power to incur expenditure out of the provision made in the approved budget and to the extent of such power shall be in accordance with the delegation of financial powers specified in schedule - F.
(2) The Zilla Panchayat shall in its meeting select 3 (three) members in addition to Adhakshaya and Up-Adhakshaya to form and Executive Committee which shall meet as often and desirable to discuss all matters other than routine administrative matters and also accord sanction wherever sanction is required to be accorded by the Executive Committee in accordance with the scheme of delegation of power specified in Schedule - F.
The Executive Committee shall be responsible for supervision of all works and scheme of Zilla Panchayat.
(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in this rule, the State Government may confer on any authority specific power to incur expenditure on specific items and upon such conferment, the said authority shall exercise such power for specified purpose only.
10. Custody, preservation of books and record & procedure for destruction. (1) The Sachiva shall ensure the safe custody of all the books of accounts and records of Zilla Panchayat and shall produce them for inspection to the auditors and any other officer/agency authorized by the Secretary. The following shall be the permanent record of Zilla Panchayat and shall be kept in record perpetually.
(a) Cash Book. (b) Bank Pass Book. (c) Annual Accounts, viz., receipts and payments account of Income and Expenditure (d) Statement and Balance Sheet. (e) Audit Report. (f) Assets Register. (2) Any other record not listed in sub-rule (2) above shall be preserved for the next 5 (five) years and thereafter, can be destroyed after their audit of accounts of that particular period that taken place as per the guidelines specified by the State Government in that behalf from time to time.
11. Audit of accounts. It shall be the duty of Adhakshya and Sachiva to get its accounts audited, whenever called upon to do so by the auditors appointment in its behalf by the State Government and extend all assistance to the auditors to facilitate examination of audit of accounts.
12. Removal of doubt. When a doubt arises as to the interpretation of any provision of these rules, the matter shall be referred to the Secretary, Rural Development Department whose decision thereon, shall be final and binding.
R.Ongmu,
Secretary to the Government of Sikkim,
Rural Development Department.

Transparency in public administration forms the cornerstone of accountability and public trust. Section 4(1)(b) of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005, mandates every public authority to proactively disclose detailed organizational data. This statutory requirement ensures that citizens have seamless access to routine administrative records without having to repeatedly file individual RTI requests.
To streamline compliance across municipal, state, and central institutions, adopting a structured, standardized, and fillable template is essential. Below is a comprehensive, end-to-end framework that public authorities can implement to fulfill all statutory requirements under Section 4(1)(b).

Overview Managing administrative tasks efficiently requires clear, formal communication—especially when requesting physical assets or tools necessary for daily operations. In a formal government or audit environment, official requisitions need to state the precise operational requirement, justify the need based on ongoing workloads, and provide technical specifications to avoid administrative delays.
Official Draft: Heavy-Duty Stapler Requisition Below is the refined format for submitting an official requisition for heavy-duty office binding equipment to the Finance Department.
To,
The Director,
Local Fund Audit / Internal Audit,
Finance Department,
Government of Sikkim, Gangtok.
Dated: 20/02/2026
Subject: Requisition for procurement of Heavy-Duty Stapler for Report Binding.
Sir,
I have the honor to bring to your kind notice that the preparation and binding of audit reports is a continuous, year-round activity within this section. Given the high volume of documents and the thickness of the annual reports, standard office equipment is insufficient for binding operations.
To ensure the professional quality, structural integrity, and durability of the bound reports, it is requested that a Heavy-Duty Stapler (with a binding capacity of approximately 100–200 sheets, suitable for 23/8 to 23/24 size staples) be sanctioned for procurement.
The acquisition of this equipment will streamline our report finalization process, eliminate reliance on external binding services, and prevent delays in official report submissions.
Submitted for your kind consideration and necessary financial/administrative approval.
Yours faithfully,
(Signature)
[Name / Designation]
[Section / Unit Name]
Best Practices for Administrative Requisitions When drafting requisitions for procurement or technical resources, incorporating the following elements helps expedite processing:
Quantify Requirements: Specify clear capacity metrics (e.g., sheet count, dimensions, or hardware load specs). Highlight Cost Efficiency: Frame the request around long-term utility or cost savings (e.g., replacing recurring external service fees with a one-time equipment purchase). Include Technical Specifications: Prevent back-and-forth inquiries by outlining necessary parameters upfront.

Introduction In the realm of public governance, ensuring financial accountability, transparency, and optimal utilization of public resources is paramount. Governments handle vast amounts of public funds, execute complex programs, and manage extensive assets. To maintain fiscal discipline and prevent irregularities, organizations rely heavily on robust oversight mechanisms. Among these, the Internal Audit Organisation acts as a crucial catalyst from within, safeguarding public funds and streamlining department functions.
This blog explores the comprehensive framework governing internal audits—drawing from foundational guidelines (such as the 1992 and 2005 supplementary regulations)—while diving deep into core concepts like internal control mechanisms and the classic performance framework known as the 3 E’s (Economy, Efficiency, and Effectiveness).
Part 1: The Blueprint of Internal Audit An internal audit is essentially an independent, objective assurance and consulting activity designed to add value and improve an organization’s operations. Within government structures, its primary role is to help departments maintain accurate records, correct mistakes early on, and eliminate later-stage objections from statutory auditors (such as the Accountant General).
Scope and Jurisdiction The purview of a modern internal audit organisation is extensive, spanning:
Government Departments & Field Offices: Checking initial accounts maintained in executive offices to verify compliance with accounting rules and financial procedures. Pay and Accounts Offices (PAOs) & DDOS: Scrutinizing payments, pay fixations, general provident fund (GPF/CPF) accounts, pensions, and loan accounts. Autonomous Bodies & Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs): Reviewing financial records of entities substantially financed by or holding government investments. Receipts & Stores Verification: Assessing revenue collections, refunds, and conducting physical verifications of store assets and equipment. Core Duties and Procedures Internal audit parties typically conduct local inspections on-site. Their duties involve a general review of all accounts since the last inspection, coupled with a detailed check of selected records. Key focus areas include:
Compliance Verification: Ensuring payments align with statutory rules and arithmetical accuracy. Sanction and Purchase Procedures: Checking that procurement rules are followed and proper justification exists for non-acceptance of lowest bids. Drafting Inspection Reports: Producing objective, fact-based reports broken into past outstanding objections (Part I) and current audit irregularities (Part II). Part 2: Demystifying Internal Control Mechanisms A recurring theme in modern audit guidelines is the evaluation of internal control. But what exactly is an internal control mechanism?
An internal control mechanism is a network of systems, policies, and procedures implemented by management to provide reasonable assurance regarding the achievement of objectives in three primary categories:
Effectiveness and Efficiency of Operations: Using resources wisely and productively. Reliability of Financial Reporting: Ensuring figures reported are accurate and trustworthy. Compliance with Laws and Regulations: Adhering strictly to statutory frameworks and internal policies. How the Internal Audit Wing Improves Internal Control Internal auditors do not just look at past errors; they evaluate the very machinery of governance. The audit wing strengthens internal controls by:
Assessing System Design: Reviewing whether existing controls are adequate, appropriate, and operating as intended. Pinpointing Weaknesses and Risks: Identifying systemic gaps, bottlenecks, or weak segregation of duties that could pave the way for fraud or defalcation. Recommending Corrective Actions: Proposing structural fixes, policy revisions, or enhanced monitoring protocols. Tracking Compliance & Follow-Up: Reviewing Action Taken Reports (ATRs) to ensure departments actively remediate vulnerabilities found during previous inspections. Part 3: The 3 E’s of Performance Audit—Economy, Efficiency, and Effectiveness When auditing programs and performance, internal auditors look beyond simple compliance and dive into the 3 E’s. This framework helps evaluate whether public money is delivering genuine value.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+| THE 3 E'S FRAMEWORK |+-------------------+--------------------+------------------------+| 1. ECONOMY | 2. EFFICIENCY | 3. EFFECTIVENESS || Minimizing input | Maximizing output | Achieving intended || costs | per unit of input | outcomes & goals |+-------------------+--------------------+------------------------+ 1. Economy Definition: Acquiring resources (inputs) of the appropriate quality and quantity at the lowest possible cost. Focus: Competitive procurement, avoiding unnecessary spending, and waste reduction. Audit Example: Checking whether a department procured office supplies or machinery by fairly evaluating competitive vendor bids rather than overspending. 2. Efficiency Definition: Maximizing the output, results, or services achieved relative to the resources (time, money, labor) consumed. It’s about getting the most “bang for your buck.” Focus: Streamlining processes, reducing administrative bottlenecks, and optimizing resource workflows. Audit Example: Assessing the cost per beneficiary served in a welfare scheme to see if administrative overhead is draining funds that should reach citizens. 3. Effectiveness Definition: Measuring the extent to which a program or policy achieves its intended objectives and outcomes. It is about doing the right things and generating real-world impact. Focus: Target achievement, impact evaluation, and strategic goal realization. Audit Example: Evaluating a public health vaccination campaign not just on whether vaccines were purchased (Economy) or administered quickly (Efficiency), but whether it successfully reduced the incidence of the targeted disease in the region (Effectiveness). Conclusion Internal auditing has evolved from a mere routine checker of bills into a strategic advisory partner for government management. By rigorously examining internal controls, upholding compliance, and evaluating performance through the lens of the 3 E’s, internal audit wings ensure that public administration remains accountable, transparent, and responsive to the needs of the public. Through systematic planning, objective reporting, and active follow-up, internal audit continues to fortify the foundation of sound public financial management.

Conducting a statutory or internal audit of local self-government institutions—such as Gram Panchayat Units (GPUs), Zilla Panchayats (ZPs), and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) or Municipalities—requires a structured, systematic approach. Auditing these bodies involves verifying not only cash transactions and bank balances but also statutory compliance, public procurement guidelines, revenue realisations, and asset registers.
This comprehensive guide compiles every essential checklist, fillable requisition format, financial reporting template, and technical explanation needed to prepare for or execute an audit of local governing bodies.
1. Statutory Framework and Audit Objectives Local bodies operate under specific state acts (such as the Sikkim Panchayat Act 1993, the Sikkim Municipalities Act 2007, and the Sikkim Local Fund Audit Act 2012) alongside Central Finance Commission guidelines. The primary objective of the audit is to ensure:
Financial Propriety: Verifying that expenditure is backed by proper sanctions, budget provisions, and valid vouchers. Revenue Optimization: Ensuring local taxes, user fees, and non-tax revenues are accurately assessed, collected, and deposited. Asset Accountability: Confirming that public infrastructure, dead stock, tools, and equipment are correctly catalogued and physically verified. Compliance and Governance: Scrutinising scheme implementation (e.g., MGNREGA, 15th FC), social audits, Gram Sabha minutes, and RTI proactive disclosures. 2. General Documents & Records Master Checklist Before an audit begins, the local body must gather primary documents, registers, procurement files, and compliance records.

Annual Financial Statements: Receipt and Payment Accounts, Income and Expenditure Accounts, and Balance Sheets. Budget Estimates: Approved Annual Budget and any supplementary estimates. Vouchers & Receipts: Chronologically organized original paid vouchers with bills, receipts, and challans. Registers & Internal Controls Imprest/Advance Registers: Tracking permanent advances and personal/impersonal pending advances. Stock & Asset Registers: Dead Stock Register, Consumable Stores Register, and Tools & Plant (T&P) Ledger. Establishment Records: Salary Audit Registers, Service Books, Attendance Registers, and Honorarium Registers. Log Books: Vehicle Log Books, history sheets, and Petrol, Oil & Lubricants (POL) usage logs. Procurement, Works, & Schemes Works Register: Master catalog of all ongoing and completed projects. Individual Work Files: Project reports, Administrative Approvals (AA), Technical Sanctions (TS), and detailed estimates. Measurement Books (MBs): Updated MBs with check-measurement entries by authorized engineers. Procurement Files: Tender notices, quotations, comparative statements, and purchase orders for stationery, furniture, and equipment. Governance & Compliance Meeting Records: Gram Sabha, Ward Sabha, or Municipal Board Meeting Minutes Registers. Previous Audits: Prior Audit Reports along with the Action Taken Report (ATR) on past objections. RTI Compliance: Proactive disclosure records as mandated under Section 4 of the RTI Act. 3. The Ultimate Guide: How to Set Up Free Remote Desktop for Windows 11 and Android Whether you need to grab a forgotten file, run heavy desktop software from your couch, or help a family member troubleshoot their PC, having remote access to your Windows 11 machine from your Android phone is an absolute game-changer.
Gone are the days when you had to pay hefty subscription fees for basic remote access. Today, there are several powerful, completely free tools that bridge the gap between your mobile device and your PC.
In this guide, we will break down the top three freeware remote desktop solutions for Windows 11 and Android, detailing exactly how to set them up for a flawless experience.
1. Chrome Remote Desktop: The Easiest Setup (Best for Most Users) Google’s Chrome Remote Desktop remains the reigning champion for everyday users. Because it operates through your Google Account, it bypasses complex firewall rules and network configurations. It just works.
Why choose it? It’s incredibly stable, requires zero technical know-how, and is completely free with no hidden tiers.
Step 1: Set Up Your Windows 11 PC Open Google Chrome: Make sure you are signed into your primary Google Account. Navigate to the portal: Go to remotedesktop.google.com/access. Install the Host: Click the Download icon located under the “Set up remote access” section. This will download a small .msi installer. Run it. Name Your PC: Choose a recognizable name (e.g., “Home Desktop”). Set a PIN: Create a secure 6-digit PIN. You will need this every time you connect from your phone. Prevent Sleep: Windows 11 PCs cannot be accessed if they go to sleep. Go to Settings > System > Power & battery and set your screen and sleep settings to “Never” while plugged in. Step 2: Connect via Your Android Device Download the App: Install the Chrome Remote Desktop app from the Google Play Store. Sign In: Ensure the app is logged into the exact same Google account used on your PC. Connect: You will see your PC’s name listed on the main screen. Tap it. Enter PIN: Input your 6-digit PIN. You can check “Don’t ask for a PIN again” for faster future access. Control: You’ll now see your desktop on your screen. You can use pinch-to-zoom and choose between touch mode (direct tapping) or trackpad mode (dragging a virtual mouse cursor). 2. RustDesk: The Open-Source Powerhouse (Best for Privacy & Performance) If you dislike relying on Google’s ecosystem or want more control over your data, RustDesk is the absolute best alternative in 2026. It is open-source, features end-to-end encryption, and is incredibly lightweight.
Why choose it? It offers features normally locked behind paywalls (like native file transfer) and doesn’t require creating an account.
Step 1: Set Up Your Windows 11 PC Download the App: Head over to rustdesk.com and download the Windows executable. Install It: When you launch the app, it runs in “portable” mode by default. For unattended, anytime access, click the “Install” button on the left-hand panel. Configure Access: On the main screen, you will see your ID and a temporary Password. Set a Permanent Password: Click the pencil icon next to the password to set a custom, permanent password. This ensures you can always log in without needing to look at the PC screen. Step 2: Connect via Your Android Device Download the App: Install RustDesk from the Play Store or their official GitHub repository. Enter the ID: On the app’s home screen, type in the remote ID displayed on your Windows PC. Connect: Tap the connect arrow. Authenticate: Enter the permanent password you set up earlier. Enjoy: RustDesk features an excellent toolbar that allows you to easily switch monitors, adjust image quality, and transfer files directly to your phone’s storage. 3. AnyViewer: The Mobile-First Experience (Best Touch Controls) AnyViewer has rapidly grown in popularity due to its focus on mobile usability. If you find navigating a desktop UI on a small phone screen frustrating, AnyViewer’s optimized touch controls and custom virtual keyboards might be your favorite choice.
Why choose it? It features “One-click control,” making connecting incredibly fast once your devices are paired.
Step 1: Set Up Your Windows 11 PC Download: Go to the AnyViewer website and download the Windows client. Create an Account: You will need to sign up for a free account. Log In: Log into the desktop app. Once logged in, your PC is automatically bound to your account and listed under the “Device” tab. Step 2: Connect via Your Android Device Download: Grab the AnyViewer app from the Google Play Store. Log In: Sign in using the same account credentials. One-Click Connect: Navigate to the Device tab at the bottom of the screen. Tap your PC’s name, and select One-click control. Navigate: Take advantage of their mobile-friendly UI, which includes quick shortcuts for Ctrl+Alt+Del, opening the task manager, and utilizing a virtual mouse. At a Glance: Which should you choose? Feature Chrome Remote Desktop RustDesk AnyViewer Account Required? Yes (Google) No Yes (AnyViewer) Ease of Setup ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ⭐⭐⭐⭐ ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ File Transfer No (Limited upload/download) Yes (Robust) Yes (Free tier limits apply) Security Focus Standard Google Security End-to-End Encryption ECC Encryption Best For… Absolute beginners Tech enthusiasts & privacy advocates Mobile power users Pro-Tips for a Flawless Setup Check Your Antivirus/Firewall: While these programs usually punch their own holes through Windows Defender, strict third-party antiviruses might block remote desktop ports. If your connection times out, temporarily disable your firewall to test if it’s the culprit, then whitelist the application. Mastering Power Settings: A sleeping PC cannot be woken up by a standard remote desktop request over the internet. You must disable sleep mode. However, you can set the display to turn off to save power and screen life. Advanced: Wake-on-LAN (WoL): If you don’t want to leave your PC running 24/7, look into enabling Wake-on-LAN. This requires going into your motherboard’s BIOS and your network adapter’s device manager settings. Once configured, apps like RustDesk can send a “Magic Packet” to boot up your PC remotely before you connect!
